events.text: You are the oldest student at the village school, the one the teacher keeps for the county examination, and every dusk you walk home by the hill road past the grave mounds. For a month now a stranger in a pale cotton jacket has walked beside you there, at arm's length, always from the same bend. They taught you a game of the hill road, an old one: a small warm bead that passes from one breath to the next, there and back, while you talk. You are paler every morning. Your brush shakes over the characters. Today the schoolmaster kept you back, looked at you for a long time, and told you an old story out loud, the one about the fox and the bead, and what the student in it was told to do. Tonight the stranger is waiting at the bend.
events.arc: The Bead on the Hill Road

choices.text: When the bead comes to you, swallow it and look at the sky

ok.log: The bead comes on the stranger's breath and you close your teeth on it and swallow, and it goes down like a hot coal. You turn your face up to the sky, as the schoolmaster said, and your foot finds a root, and you fall flat on the road with your face in the dust. When you open your eyes you are looking at the earth: and you can see it. The veins of the hill under the grass, cold and warm, where the water runs and where the dead lie easy. Behind you there is a cry like a vixen's in winter, and then nothing. You never see the stranger again. You never see the sky that way either. People will know the earth from you, and not heaven.

fail.log: You swallow it and look up, and the sky is right there, enormous, and for one breath you almost understand it. Then you trip on the stranger's sleeve and fall on your face, and when you open your eyes you are staring at a beetle on a clod of earth and you know, absolutely, which way the water under the hill runs. The stranger is gone. The bead is in you, small and cold now. You will be good at graves and wells for the rest of your life, and you will always wonder what the sky would have said. (-5 health)

choices.text: Give it back, and say: I know what you are

effects.log: When the bead comes to you, you take it out of your mouth with two fingers and hold it out on your open palm. "I know," you say. "The schoolmaster told me the story." The stranger looks at the bead, and at you, for a long time. Then they take it, very carefully, without touching your hand, and walk away down the hill road into the grass. Where they stood, on the road, there is one red-brown hair, long and fine. You keep it. Your colour comes back in a week.

choices.text: Bring the schoolmaster's dogs to the bend

effects.log: You come to the bend with the schoolmaster's two yellow dogs on a rope. They go mad. The stranger turns their head toward the noise, and for one breath the face is wrong, too long, the eyes catching the last of the light, and then there is nobody on the road at all, only the silver grass moving where nothing is. From somewhere up among the grave mounds, something laughs, a short sharp bark of a laugh. The dogs will not go up that hill again. Neither, for a while, will you.

events.text: You followed the bigger children up to the old graves to look for chestnuts and they ran off and left you, and now it is dusk and every grave mound looks like every other. The grass is taller than you. Somewhere a dog barks, far below, and you cannot tell where. Then, between two mounds, a small light comes on, low to the ground, like a lantern carried by someone very short. Under it is a red-brown fox with a white chest, looking at you. The light is on the end of its tail.
events.arc: The Bead on the Hill Road

choices.text: Follow the light

effects.log: It trots ahead, not fast, and stops at every turn until you catch up. Down between the mounds, over the little ditch, along the dyke between the paddies. At the village gate it sits down in the road, and the light on its tail goes out like a pinched wick, and it is just a fox, and then it is not there at all. Nobody believes you. The grown-ups say you were dreaming on your feet. You know where the light stopped, though: exactly where the lantern-post is.

choices.text: Throw a stone at it

effects.log: You throw a stone, because you are frightened and it is the only thing you can think of. You miss by a long way. The fox looks at the stone, and then at you, in a way that makes your face hot. Then it turns and trots off between the mounds with its light, and stops, and waits. You follow it, in the end, because there is nothing else to do, and it takes you all the way to the village gate, and at the gate it sneezes at you, once, and is gone.

choices.text: Bow to it, the way you bow to the old people

effects.log: You put your hands together and bow, very low, the way you were taught to bow to the old people at New Year. The fox sits up. It looks, for one moment, astonished. Then it bows back, or seems to, dipping its head over its white chest, and leads you down the hill with its light. At the village gate you say thank you out loud. In the morning there is a chestnut on your doorstep, a big one, already peeled.

events.text: A rich farming house in the next county has hired you, because a cow dies in its shed every night and the hired men say a ghost. The cows have no marks on them. They are simply cold in the morning. The youngest son of the house says they die of looking at the moon. {npc}, the eldest son, driven out years ago for saying what {he} saw, has come back up the road in a monk's grey with four small bottles at {his} belt: yellow, white, blue, red. "A monk gave me these," {npc} says. "Watch the shed at the full moon. Then decide whose side you are on." At the full moon you watch. The daughter of the house, the one the family prayed for, crosses the yard to the shed in a white jacket. The shadow on the shed wall is the wrong shape.
events.arc: The Bead on the Hill Road

choices.text: Help {npc}: run with the four bottles

ok.log: You and {npc} run, and the daughter comes after you down the dark road faster than anyone should run. {npc} throws the yellow bottle and a hill of boulders stands up across the road; the white, and a thicket of thorns; the blue, and a river. The daughter comes through all of them. You throw the last one yourself, the red, and the road behind you goes up in a wall of fire, and out of the fire, very small, rises something no bigger than a mosquito, and whines away into the summer dark. The cattle stop dying. The family does not thank either of you.

fail.log: You run with {npc} and the daughter comes after you, and you fumble the bottles, and the blue one breaks on your own boot and drenches you to the waist in a river that was not there. {npc} throws the red one over your head. Fire, and in the fire something very small rising and whining away into the dark. You lie in the wet road laughing like a fool, and {npc}, at last, laughs too. (-8 health)

choices.text: Go to the well and sit with the daughter, and ask what the daughter wants

effects.log: You find the daughter at the well, sitting on its stone lip, and you sit down at the other end of it, a long way off, and ask. The daughter looks at you a long time with eyes that catch the moon. "To be real," comes the answer. "They asked heaven for a daughter, even a fox. Heaven heard. Two more, and I would be real." You say that the cattle are not the daughter's to take. No answer. In the morning the daughter is gone from the house, and {npc} is gone down the road, and the cattle stop dying, and you never know which of them you saved.

choices.text: Guard the cowshed and do nothing else

effects.log: You sit in the cowshed doorway with your sword across your knees and do not move until dawn. The daughter comes to the yard, and sees you, and stands in the moonlight a long while, and goes back in. Not one cow dies. Not that night, or the next twenty. The family pays you double and believes, to this day, that you frightened off a ghost. {npc} walks away down the road with four full bottles, shaking {his} head.

events.text: The wine-house at the crossroads below the pass is the best on the road: the makgeolli is cold, the soup has real radish greens in it, and the keeper remembers every traveller's name from one year to the next. Tonight, as the keeper sets down your bowl, you see on the dark sleeve one long hair, fine and red-brown, the colour of no human head. Out in the yard a stranger's yellow dog has been barking at the kitchen door since dusk, and will not stop. The dog's master, a hunter with a falcon's hood on his belt, has gone up to the pass and said he will be back with questions. The keeper's eyes meet yours. They catch the lamp, the way an animal's do.
events.arc: The Bead on the Hill Road

choices.text: Pay, thank the keeper, and say nothing

effects.log: You pay, a little over. You thank the keeper for the soup, which was very good. You say nothing about sleeves. The keeper looks at you a long moment and then says your name, which you never gave, and wishes you a safe road. Every time you come back down that road for the rest of your life, there is a bowl of cold makgeolli on the table before you have sat down.

choices.text: Lean close and tell the keeper the hunter is coming back

effects.log: "The hunter with the dog is coming back with questions," you say, very low, looking at your soup. The keeper goes still. Then picks the red-brown hair off the sleeve, quite slowly, and drops it into the lamp, where it fizzes. "Thank you," the keeper says. In the morning the wine-house has a new keeper, older, with a different face and the same soup, and the yellow dog lies in the yard with its chin on its paws and does not bark at all.

choices.text: Go up to the pass and tell the hunter what you saw

effects.log: You find the hunter at the top of the pass and tell him. He thanks you very civilly and goes down with the dog. By the time he gets there the wine-house is dark and the keeper is gone, and the dog runs three times round the yard and then sits down in the road and howls at the hill. The crossroads has no good soup for a year. You find that you mind that more than you expected.

events.text: You are walking alone on the high mountain at dusk, on a path you have never seen before, between pines so old their bark has gone grey as stone. A black fox with a white muzzle is sitting in the middle of the path, older than any sect on the mountain, older than the mountain's name. It speaks in a voice like dry leaves turning over. "A thousand years ago a voice from heaven told me I might be born human," it says, "if one human, freely, wrote me a poem. I have waited. I will not lie to you about what I did while I waited. Will you write?" There is a brush and an inkstone on a flat rock beside it, and paper, very old.
events.arc: The Bead on the Hill Road

choices.text: Write the poem

ok.log: You write it in one breath: smoke round a lonely grave, a pelt laid down like an old robe, a road that goes up the hill and does not come back down. When you lift the brush the fox reads it for a long time. Its eyes are wet. It takes the paper in its mouth, very gently, folds it with its paws as neatly as any clerk, bows to you until its white muzzle touches the stone, and walks off down a path that closes behind it like water. Wherever it went, it went with your poem.

fail.log: You write it, and it is clumsy: a rhyme that does not land, a line about the moon that every bad poet in the world has written. You know it. You are about to tear it up when the fox puts a paw on the paper. "It is given freely," it says. "Heaven did not say good." It folds the clumsy poem as if it were a king's letter, takes it in its mouth, bows, and is gone. You are embarrassed about that poem for the rest of your life, and proud of it, both.

choices.text: Ask it first what it did while it waited

effects.log: It tells you. It does not make it prettier. Breaths it took from sleepers, and how many of them woke pale and how many did not wake; the faces it wore; the one it loved and left; the years it went hungry rather than do the old thing the stories name. It takes until the moon is down. Then you write, and the poem you write is not kind, and it is not cruel, and every word of it is true. The fox reads it and makes a sound you have never heard an animal make, and takes it, and bows, and goes.

choices.text: Refuse

effects.log: "No," you say. "Not freely. I would be writing because I am afraid of you, and that would be a lie." The fox looks at you for a long while with its old wet eyes. Then it bows, exactly as low as it would have bowed for the poem, and turns, and walks away down the path, and when you look again the path is not there. You go back by that rock a dozen times in the years after. It is only a rock.

events.text: A few years after the poem on the cloud-island, you find on your doorstep in heaven a folded paper, very old, with your own handwriting on it. Under it there is a single black hair with a white tip. The paper has been read so often its folds are soft as cloth. Somebody has written on the back, in a careful hand that is not quite human: "Still waiting. Better company now."
events.arc: The Bead on the Hill Road

choices.text: Write an answer on the back and leave it on the step

effects.log: You write one line, and leave it on the step under a stone. In the morning it is gone, and on the step is a pine cone, perfectly ordinary, which smells, faintly, of grave earth and of the moon. You keep it on your desk until the end of your very long life.

choices.text: Keep the paper, and go looking for the pines

effects.log: You go looking. The cloud-island is where it was, but the pines are gone, and in their place is a small round mound of earth with grass on it, such as people below make for their dead. You sit by it a while. It does not feel like a grave. It feels like a door, closed politely, with someone home.

events.text: Since the night on the hill road you cannot walk across a field without knowing things about it. This spring a family in the village is digging a new well in the wrong place: you can feel the water, cold and fast, three paces to the left and a man's height down. They are already waist deep in dry clay.
events.arc: The One Who Looked at the Earth

choices.text: Tell them where the water is

effects.log: They laugh, and then, because the clay is very dry, they try it. Water at a man's height, cold and fast, exactly there. By autumn three villages have asked you where to dig. You stop saying that a fox told you. Nobody would believe it, and it is not quite true: the fox only told you to look up.

choices.text: Say nothing: it frightens you

effects.log: You walk past. They dig for four days and find nothing and give up, and dig, in the end, exactly three paces to the left, because the old grandmother of the house dreamed it. You lie awake. The thing in you is not going away. It is going to keep telling you where the water is whether you want it or not.

choices.text: Ask the schoolmaster what is happening to you

effects.log: The schoolmaster pours you tea and listens and does not seem surprised. "The story says sky, earth, and people," the old teacher says. "You looked at the earth. Many great geomancers began on a hill road, if you believe the villages. Most of them stumbled." A pause. "Study the classics anyway. The earth will not teach you to write a letter."

events.text: The eldest son of a great family has come with a geomancer's compass of his own and a purse, to ask you to choose his father's grave. Two other geomancers have chosen two other hills. You walk all three. On the first, the earth is sour. On the second, it is good. On the third, the earth is so good it hums under your feet, and somebody's old grave mound is already on it: a poor family's, the grass uncut.
events.arc: The One Who Looked at the Earth

choices.text: Choose the second hill, and leave the poor family's grave alone

effects.log: You choose the second hill and say it is the best. It is not the best. It is the best that does not need a poor family's grandmother moved. The great family's sons do well enough. The poor family's sons, you hear years later, do rather better than anyone expected.

choices.text: Tell the truth: the third hill, and who lies there

effects.log: You tell him exactly what you feel under each hill, and whose grave is on the third. The eldest son is quiet a long time. Then he takes the second hill, and sends a man to cut the grass on the poor family's mound at Chuseok every year after, without telling them who. You think the fox would have liked that.

choices.text: Choose the third hill for him: the family can be paid to move

effects.log: The poor family is paid and the old grave is moved and the great family's father goes into the humming earth. You are paid twenty taels. That winter the earth under your own feet goes quiet for three months, as if someone had stopped speaking to you, and you understand that what you were given can be taken back.

events.text: You are old, and known in three provinces as the geomancer who never chose a bad site, and one evening you walk the hill road past the grave mounds again for the first time in decades. At the bend, in the silver grass, an old fox with a grey muzzle is sitting, thin, with no light on its tail at all. It looks at you. It is waiting for something.
events.arc: The One Who Looked at the Earth

choices.text: Sit down at arm's length and tell it what you saw in the earth

effects.log: You tell it about the wells and the graves and the veins of the hills, all of it, the whole long life that came out of one fall on this road. The fox listens with its ears forward. When the moon is up it gets to its feet, stiffly, and touches its nose once to the dust where you fell, decades ago, and goes off into the grass. It looked, you think, as if it had been told the end of a story it began.

choices.text: Offer it back, if it can be given back

effects.log: "If you want it," you say, "take it." The old fox looks at you a long time and shakes its head, a very human shake. Then it lies down in the grass at the side of the road, near you, and the two of you watch the moon come up together until it is time to go home. Neither of you asked the other for anything more.

events.text: You still keep the red-brown hair from the hill road, folded in a twist of paper inside the Thousand Character Classic. Tonight the paper is warm when you touch it, as warm as a hand, and outside, on the road below the house, a pale jacket is standing in the dark, at a polite distance, not coming nearer.

choices.text: Go out and stand at arm's length, and wait

effects.log: You go out and stand where you stood on the hill road. The stranger does not come closer. "You knew," they say, "and you gave it back. Nobody gives it back." Then they tell you, quietly, that there is a student at the next village's school who has started walking home by the graves, and that you might mention the story to them. Then they are gone. You do. The student, for once, listens.

choices.text: Burn the hair in the lamp

effects.log: You burn it. It fizzes and smells of autumn. The figure on the road bows, very slightly, the way one bows to someone who has closed a door politely, and walks away. You sleep well for the first time in weeks, and in the morning you are a little sorry.

choices.text: Call softly that you would like to know their name

effects.log: There is a silence so long you think they have gone. Then a voice from the dark says a name, a plain village name, the kind a grandmother would have, and adds: "That is the one I am using this year." It is the most honest thing anyone has ever said to you.

events.text: You have become, somehow, the person in the district who tells students the old story. Every autumn a new one comes to your gate, pale, with a shaking brush hand and a tale of a stranger on a road. This year's is very young, and very proud, and says the stranger is the only person who has ever understood them.

choices.text: Tell the story, all of it, and let them choose

effects.log: You tell it: the bead, the breath, the paleness, the fall and the earth, the giving back. You do not tell them what to do. A week later the student comes back with colour in their face and a single red-brown hair in a twist of paper, and you take yours out of the Classic, and you laugh together until the schoolmaster comes to see what the noise is.

choices.text: Walk the road with them at dusk

ok.log: You walk the hill road with the student at dusk, and at the bend the pale jacket is waiting, and sees you, and stops. You nod to it. It nods back, a long, tired, almost amused nod, and turns off into the grass and does not come to that road again. The student is furious with you for a month and grateful for the rest of their life.

fail.log: The student will not walk with you. You go alone, and at the bend there is nobody at all, and you feel foolish. But the next morning the student is at your gate, white as rice paper, and says that the stranger asked them, last night, whether they knew you, and then walked away.

events.text: Since the evening with the dogs, something on the hill has taken an interest in you. Your straw sandals are found in the morning set neatly on the roof. Your ink turns out to have been watered. Once, at the school, a whole page of your characters has been very slightly improved, overnight, in a hand better than yours.

choices.text: Leave a rice cake on the hill road as a peace offering

effects.log: The rice cake is gone by morning. In its place is your missing ink-stick. The tricks stop, or nearly: once a year, at the first full moon, your sandals are still on the roof. You come to look forward to it.

choices.text: Keep the dogs at your door

effects.log: The dogs sleep at your door. The tricks stop. The dogs grow fat and lazy and, you suspect, are being fed by something on the hill road that wants them fat and lazy. You decide not to think about it too hard.

choices.text: Study the improved characters, and learn from them

effects.log: You copy the improved characters a hundred times each, the way the school teaches. Your hand gets better. The improvements get subtler. At the examination, the next spring, the examiner remarks that your brush has a curious old-fashioned elegance, as if you had learned from a very old master. You do not explain.

events.text: A hunting party is going up the hill with dogs and torches: the headman has offered a sack of rice for the fox of the grave mounds, because a hen has gone missing. They ask you, as the one who brought the dogs that time, to lead them to the bend.

choices.text: Lead them the long way round, to nowhere

effects.log: You lead them up and round and through every bramble on the hill until midnight, and down again, sore and empty-handed. The hen turns up next day in the miller's yard. That night your sandals are on the roof again, both of them, and between them, very neatly, a single chestnut.

choices.text: Lead them to the bend

effects.log: You lead them to the bend. The dogs go mad and then go silent and lie down whimpering. Nothing is there. From far up the hill, among the mounds, comes a short sharp bark of a laugh, the same one, and the headman's torch goes out by itself. Nobody suggests the hill again.

choices.text: Tell them about the hen in the miller's yard

effects.log: "Ask the miller," you say. They do, grumbling. The hen is in the miller's yard. The hunting party goes home. You feel, walking back past the hill, that something up there is very pleased with you, and very slightly disappointed.

events.text: {npc}, the old schoolmaster who told you the story, is dying, and has sent for you. In the little room behind the school the window looks out over the hill road. "I want to tell you something I never told you," {npc} says. "When I was a student, on that road, I was given the same bead. I gave it back. I have wondered for sixty years whether I should have swallowed it."

choices.text: Tell the teacher what your choice gave you

effects.log: You tell it plainly, what came of your night on the road, the good and the bad. {npc} listens with eyes closed. "Then we both chose," {npc} says, "and neither of us chose the sky." A laugh, small and dry. "Perhaps nobody does. Perhaps that is the point of the story." {npc} dies that winter, and the whole village walks the hill road behind the bier.

choices.text: Ask whether the stranger was the same one

effects.log: {npc} smiles. "I hope so," comes the answer. "I should like to think there is someone on that road who has known me since I was sixteen." Then, after a long silence: "Go and walk the road sometimes, when I am dead. Somebody should keep it company."

events.text: Every child in the village knows now that you were led home by a fox with a light on its tail, and none of them believe it, and all of them want to go and see. Tonight three of them have dared you to take them up to the graves after dark.

choices.text: Take them up, and tell them to be quiet and polite

effects.log: You go up with a paper lantern and three children who are much less brave than they said. At the top you all sit in a row on the grass, very quietly and very politely, and after a long while a small light comes on far off among the mounds, and goes out, and comes on again, like someone waving. Nobody says a word all the way home. Nobody ever calls you a liar again.

choices.text: Refuse: it is not a show

effects.log: "It is not a show," you say, in exactly the voice the headman uses, and they go off muttering. In the morning there is a chestnut on your doorstep, already peeled. It is not proof of anything. You keep it until it goes hard as a pebble, and then you keep it anyway.

choices.text: Go up alone with a rice cake

effects.log: You go up alone, frightened, with a rice cake in a cloth. You leave it on the flat stone at the foot of the oldest mound and say thank you to the dark. Nothing comes. In the morning the cloth is folded, neatly, in a square, which no animal could do.

events.text: Grown now, you are crossing the old graves at dusk for Chuseok, carrying a sickle to cut the summer grass off your family's mounds, when you hear a child crying somewhere among the mounds. Lost, by the sound of it. And between two mounds, low to the ground, a small light has come on.

choices.text: Stand still and let the light do it

effects.log: You stand very still, sickle down, and watch the little light go bobbing to the crying, and stop, and then come back down the hill slowly, with a small child stumbling after it. At the bottom it goes out. The child runs to you. You take them home. You do not say anything about the light. They will, for years, and nobody will believe them, and one day they will come to you.

choices.text: Go to the child yourself, and nod to the light as you pass

effects.log: You go up through the grass to the child, and on the way you pass the light, and nod to it, and it dips, the way a lantern dips when someone bows holding it. You carry the child down. When you look back, two lights are among the mounds now, one large and one very small and wobbly, as if somebody were teaching.

events.text: {npc} turns up at your door with one empty cord where the four bottles used to hang, and a jar of wine. "The monk who gave me those bottles wants them filled again," {npc} says, "and says there are three more houses in three more counties where the cattle die. I am too old to run. You are not."

choices.text: Go with {npc} to the first house

ok.log: The first house is a false alarm: a sick well, not a fox. The second is a fox, and a frightened one, young, that runs at the first sight of {npc}'s grey robe and never comes back. You do not need a single bottle. {npc} says that is the best kind of year, and pours the wine.

fail.log: The first house is a fox, and you run, and it is faster than the one before, and you lose a bottle in a ditch and your boot in a river. You come out of it alive and soaked, and so do the cattle, and so, {npc} insists, does the fox. (-6 health)

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether the foxes ever stop

effects.log: {npc} drinks and thinks. "The monk says the houses stop," {npc} says at last. "Families that pray for a daughter, even a fox. When they stop praying for even a fox, the foxes stop coming." You both sit with that a long while.

choices.text: Refuse: one house was enough

effects.log: {npc} nods as if expecting it, and leaves the wine anyway. You hear, a year later, that {npc} went alone and came home with three empty bottles and a limp and a very strange story, and told it at every wine-house between the two counties.

events.text: {npc} is dying, old, in a temple room, with four empty bottles in a row on the windowsill catching the sun. "There is a thing I never said," {npc} tells you. "That first night, when the fire went up and the little thing rose out of it. I was glad. And I was sorry. That was my sister for eighteen years."

choices.text: Say that both are allowed

effects.log: "Both are allowed," you say. {npc} closes {his} eyes, and the face goes easy, as if a rope had been untied. That summer, at the funeral, a mosquito keeps landing on the bier and will not be brushed off, and you let it stay.

choices.text: Take one bottle to keep

effects.log: {npc} presses the red bottle into your hand. Empty, it is still warm. You keep it on your own windowsill for the rest of your life, and in the long evenings of summer it hums, very faintly, like something small and far away.

events.text: Some time after the house where the cattle died, a girl in a white jacket stops you on a ferry crossing, and asks, politely, whether you remember a well. She has the same eyes. "Two more," she says, "is what I told you. I did not take them. It has been a hard year. I wanted someone to know."

choices.text: Tell her you are glad, and mean it

effects.log: "I am glad," you say. "Truly." She looks at you as if nobody has ever said that to her. When the ferry lands she is not on it, and nobody saw her get off. On the bench where she sat there is a white jacket, folded, and on the jacket a single red-brown hair. You leave it there. It was not given to you; it was left for the next person to know.

choices.text: Ask her what she will do instead

effects.log: "Wait," she says. "There is an old way that takes, and a long way that does not. The long way is a thousand days of harming no one. I am on day three hundred." She smiles, very slightly. "It is a long time to be hungry." At the landing, she is gone.

choices.text: Keep your hand on your sword and say nothing

effects.log: You say nothing. She nods, as if that were also an answer, and turns to watch the river. When the ferry lands she is not on it. You are ashamed of your hand on your sword for a long time afterward, and you are not sure you should be.

events.text: Years on, in a far county, a village is telling a new story: a stranger came to live among them, a quiet person who mended nets and never ate meat, and on the thousandth day of living there, the stranger's shadow on the paper door was, at last, the right shape. The villagers think it is a story about a ghost. You think it is not.

choices.text: Go to the far county and see

effects.log: You go. The net-mender is old now, and sits on a bench in the sun, and looks at you over the nets with eyes that are perfectly ordinary, brown and a little tired. "I remember a well," says the net-mender. "I think. It is going, the remembering. They say it goes, when you are real." You sit on the bench together a long while, mending.

choices.text: Let it be a ghost story

effects.log: You let them tell it as a ghost story. It is better that way, safer, for whoever it is. But that night you pour a cup of wine onto the ground for a person who waited a thousand days, and the wine soaks in very quickly, as if the earth were thirsty.

events.text: The rich family of the house where the cattle died has written to you. The cattle have lived. The daughter of the house is grown and kind and thin, and eats almost nothing, and sits at the cowshed door at every full moon, looking at the cattle. The family wants you to come back and guard the shed again, just in case.

choices.text: Go back, and talk to the daughter this time

effects.log: You go, and at the full moon you sit at one end of the cowshed step and the daughter at the other. You ask nothing. After a long while the daughter says, "I am trying." You say, "I know." You sit there until dawn. The cattle are fine. Something in the house is, too, for the first time.

choices.text: Go back, and guard the shed, as before

effects.log: You sit in the doorway with your sword across your knees. The daughter comes at midnight and stands in the moonlight, and goes in again. The family pays you ten taels. It is easy money and it feels like a cage, for both of you.

choices.text: Write back: it is not the cattle that need guarding

effects.log: You write: feed the daughter of the house, and stop asking heaven for anything more. The family is offended. But a year later a second letter comes, from the daughter, in a hand like a scholar's: "They listened. I am eating rice. It is not what I wanted. It is enough."

events.text: Word comes that the rich family is gone: the old parents died of age, in their beds, peacefully, and the daughter of the house buried them properly, cut the grass on their mounds at Chuseok, gave the cattle to the village, and walked away up the mountain one morning without a word. The village wants to know if you think she was a fox.

choices.text: Say: she was their daughter

effects.log: "She was their daughter," you say. "She buried them. She cut the grass." The village thinks about that, and decides you are right, and the story they tell afterwards is about a good daughter who went to be a nun. Up on the mountain, you like to think, someone is pleased with the story.

choices.text: Say nothing, and go and cut the grass on the parents' mounds yourself next Chuseok

effects.log: You go at Chuseok with a sickle. The grass on the two mounds is already cut, very neatly, and a bowl of rice is set on the flat stone, still warm, and there are small prints in the dew leading up the hill. You add your own bowl and go home.

events.text: You come down the pass again years later, and the wine-house at the crossroads is still there. The keeper has a different face now, older, a different name painted on the lantern. The soup has the same radish greens in it. The keeper sets down your bowl, and says your name, which you have not given.

choices.text: Say: the soup is as good as ever

effects.log: "As good as ever," you say. The keeper smiles, and for one moment, in the lamplight, there is something about the eyes. Then it is just a keeper again, wiping the table. On the kitchen wall, among the charcoal tally-marks of the makgeolli owed, you see your own name, years old, crossed out. Paid. You do not remember paying.

choices.text: Ask, quietly, how many faces there have been

effects.log: The keeper sits down across from you, which no keeper does. "Eleven," the keeper says. "Eleven faces, one wine-house. Every one of them has fed people and sent them home." A pause. "You are the only one who ever asked. Most people just come back."

choices.text: Stay a week and help in the kitchen

effects.log: You stay a week, splitting wood, carrying water, stirring the great soup pot. The keeper never eats in front of you and never sleeps when you are awake, and the yellow dogs of passing hunters bark at the kitchen door every night, and the keeper gives every one of them a bone. When you leave, there is a jar of makgeolli in your pack you did not put there.

events.text: The hunter with the falcon's hood, grey now, is at the next table in the wine-house at the crossroads. His yellow dog, a grandchild of the first, lies under the table with its eyes on the kitchen door. The hunter looks at you and says, very low: "You know, don't you. You knew that first night."

choices.text: Say: I know the soup is good and the travellers get home

effects.log: "I know the soup is good," you say, "and everyone who stops here gets home." The hunter looks at the kitchen door a long time. Then he puts his hand on the dog's head, and the dog lies down. "Thirty years I have hunted foxes," he says. "I have never once been fed by one." He orders another bowl.

choices.text: Say nothing, and pay for his wine

effects.log: You pay for his wine without a word. He drinks it and goes. In the morning, on the step, the keeper is giving his old yellow dog a bone, and the dog is wagging, and the hunter, at the gate, is pretending not to see.

events.text: The hunter you told about the wine-house keeper has come looking for you. He did not catch the fox. He has, he says, been thinking. "For one whole year that crossroads had no wine-house, and two travellers froze on the pass that winter who would have stopped there." He looks at his hands. "I would like you to tell me whether we did right."

choices.text: Say no

effects.log: "No," you say. He nods, as if it is what he came for. The next autumn he and you, together, build a lean-to of logs on the pass with a fire-pit and a store of wood, and nobody freezes there again. Some winters, the wood store has been filled by somebody else, very neatly.

choices.text: Say you do not know

effects.log: "I do not know," you say. "It was a fox. It was also a keeper." He laughs, unhappily. "That is what my dog thinks too," he says. "It barks, and then it wags. It has never been able to decide."

events.text: A wine-house has opened again at the crossroads below the pass. Nobody knows the keeper. The soup has radish greens in it. When you walk in, the keeper looks up, and goes still, and you understand that you are known.

choices.text: Sit down and order soup

effects.log: You sit and order soup. It comes. It is very good. The keeper watches you eat every mouthful, from across the room, and when you pay, says: "Tell your hunter the soup is on the house." You were forgiven, you think, somewhere between the first mouthful and the last. Or you were fed anyway, which may be the same thing.

choices.text: Leave, and leave them in peace

effects.log: You put a coin on the table and leave without ordering. Outside, on the road, you hear behind you the keeper's voice calling a cheerful goodnight to somebody else. It is the right sound for a crossroads. You did not deserve to hear it, and you are glad you did.

events.text: On the high mountain, years after the poem, you come upon an old grave mound with an earth dug under it, the kind foxes make. Just inside the entrance, out of the rain, is a folded paper. You know your own brush strokes even from here.

choices.text: Leave it exactly where it is

effects.log: You leave it. It has been read so often that the folds are soft as cloth. It is not yours any more. Going down the mountain, you feel lighter than you have in years, as if a poem, once given, keeps giving a little back to whoever wrote it.

choices.text: Add a line to it

ok.log: You add one line at the end, small, in better ink. It is the line the poem always lacked. When you come by a year later the paper is folded the other way, and under your new line, in a careful hand that is not quite human, someone has written: Yes.

fail.log: You add a line, and it is worse than the poem, which you would not have thought possible. You fold it back and leave it. A year later, the line has been very neatly scratched out by something with a claw. Fair.

events.text: A young person comes to your gate with a story: their grandmother was born on the high mountain, they say, of no one anyone knew, found as a small child sleeping by an old grave mound with a folded paper in her fist. She grew up kind and lived long and was never once sick. Before she died she gave the paper to her grandchild and said: take it to the person who wrote it.

choices.text: Take the paper, and read it

effects.log: It is your poem. Worn, soft as cloth. At the bottom, very faint, someone has added two characters in a child's unsteady hand: thank you. You hold it a long time. The young person waits, politely, and you find you have a great deal to tell them about their grandmother's family on the mountain.

choices.text: Tell them to keep it

effects.log: "It is yours," you say. "It was always meant to be given away." They fold it back and put it inside their jacket, against their heart, and bow. Watching them go down your road, you notice, just for a moment, that their shadow is perfectly ordinary, and that you had been looking.

events.text: You still remember everything the black fox told you on the mountain path, all night, before you wrote. Some of it you have never been able to put down. Tonight, in a wine-house in the capital, you hear a famous storyteller tell the old story of the fox and the hundred students, and laugh at the fox, and the whole room laughs with them.
events.arc: What It Did While It Waited

choices.text: Stand up and tell the room what the fox told you

ok.log: You stand up and tell them: the hungry years, the one it left, the old way it would not take. You tell it plainly. The room goes quiet, and then quieter, and the storyteller, who is no fool, sits down and listens with everyone else. Nobody laughs at the fox again in that wine-house. You hear years later that the storyteller tells your version now.

fail.log: You stand up and start, and the room is drunk and does not want a sad fox. They shout you down. But in the corner an old woman who has listened to every word nods to you, once, and when you look again her seat is empty and there is a red-brown hair on the bench.

choices.text: Let them laugh, and go home and write it down

effects.log: You go home and write it all down, everything the fox told you, as plainly as it was told. It takes you a winter. You show it to nobody. But you sleep better for it, and in the spring there is a pine cone on your desk that you did not put there.

events.text: A grave student, fierce and young, has read your account of the black fox, and come to argue. "You made it sound sorry," they say. "It drained sleepers for a thousand years. You wrote it a poem."
events.arc: What It Did While It Waited

choices.text: Say: I wrote it a true poem

effects.log: "A true poem," you say, "is not a pardon. It is a true poem." The student argues for an hour and goes away unconvinced. Ten years later the student, no longer young, writes to you: they have just been asked for a poem by someone they do not forgive. They wrote a true one.

choices.text: Agree that it was terrible, and that you wrote it anyway

effects.log: "It was terrible," you say. "And I wrote it anyway. Both are true." The student stares, and then, unwillingly, laughs. "That is the most annoying answer I have ever heard," they say. "I shall be thinking about it for years." They do.

events.text: You have gone back to the rock on the mountain a dozen times since you refused. It is only a rock. This year, though, there is a brush on it, a new one, and a fresh inkstone, and a sheet of paper weighted with a pebble, as if someone had set them out for anyone who passed. There is no fox.
events.arc: The Path That Was Not There

choices.text: Write something now, freely

effects.log: You write: not a poem for a fox, but a poem about refusing one, and about the years of wondering. It is better than anything you could have written then. You leave it under the pebble. In the morning the paper is gone, and on the rock there is a single black hair, white at the tip.

choices.text: Leave the brush untouched

effects.log: You leave it. Your answer was your answer. Walking down, you hear behind you, very faint and far up the mountain, something like laughter and something like a sigh, both at once, and you think it was the sound of being respected.

events.text: Old Grandmother Yun from the next house, who is ninety and has buried two husbands and all her teeth, catches you by the sleeve as you pass. "You go up by the graves," she says. "I have seen you. Listen. If anyone calls your name twice up there after dark, do not answer the second time. The first is a person. The second is a fox."

choices.text: Ask her how she knows

effects.log: "Because I answered," she says, and laughs her toothless laugh. "When I was sixteen. It took me three days to find my way home, and I came back with a fox's hair in my plait and the best luck in the village for a year. Do not answer. Unless you want the luck. Then answer, and take a rice cake."

choices.text: Laugh, and promise you will not answer

effects.log: You laugh and promise. Grandmother Yun does not laugh. She holds your sleeve a moment longer, and lets it go, and says, "Good. They are not wicked. Only hungry, and very bored." She goes back to her beans.

choices.text: Thank her, and bring her a bowl of your rice

effects.log: You bring her a bowl of rice. She eats it slowly with her gums and tells you, in return, every story she knows about the hill: the light on the tail, the hat that was not a hat, the stranger on the school road. It takes until dark. Walking home past the hill, you keep your mouth firmly shut.

events.text: Coming home late past the graves, with the moon not yet up, you hear your name called from up among the mounds. A voice you almost know. You stop. A moment later it calls again, exactly the same, the same breath in the same place. Grandmother Yun's rule comes back to you.

choices.text: Do not answer the second time; walk on

effects.log: You walk on, very steadily, not too fast. Behind you on the hill something sighs, quite loudly, like a child told no. At home you find a burr in your sleeve that you did not walk through. You tell Grandmother Yun in the morning and she slaps her knee and cackles.

choices.text: Answer, and take the luck

ok.log: "Here!" you call. There is a delighted silence. You find your way home only at dawn, by a road you have never seen, with a red-brown hair in your sleeve. That year every seed you plant comes up, every coin you drop lands face up, and every dog in the village growls at you. Fair trade.

fail.log: "Here!" you call, and walk in circles among the mounds until dawn, through every bramble on the hill, and come home scratched and soaked. At the door there is a rice cake on the step, a little bitten. You feel you were laughed at, generously. (-5 health)

events.text: Grandmother Yun has died, very old, and the whole village carries her bier up the hill road to the graves. At the edge of the pines, while the mourners wail, you see a red-brown fox sitting perfectly still, watching, with its head bowed.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let it mourn

effects.log: You say nothing. When the mound is raised and the mourners go down, the fox comes and sits on the new earth a moment, and lays something on it, and goes. You go and look: a chestnut, peeled. You leave it there. She would have liked that.

choices.text: Nudge the person next to you, and point

effects.log: They look, and see it, and their mouth falls open, and then the whole funeral is looking, and the fox, very dignified, gets up and walks off into the pines. Afterwards the village tells it as a great honour: even the foxes of the hill came to Grandmother Yun's funeral. They are right.

events.text: You set horsehair snares along the paddy dyke for hares, the way an old trapper taught you, and this morning one of them has a fox in it: red-brown, white chest, one foreleg caught. It does not struggle. It looks at you with eyes that are far too patient, and then, quite clearly, at the knife at your belt.

choices.text: Cut it free

effects.log: You cut the horsehair. The fox does not run at once. It sits on the dyke and licks its leg and looks at you, and then it trots off along the frost, stopping once to look back. You have the oddest feeling it was memorising your face.

choices.text: Cut it free, and say: come back and see me

effects.log: "Come back and see me," you say, feeling silly, and cut the snare. The fox looks at you very hard. Then it dips its head and goes. All that winter, now and then, there is a fox at the far end of the dyke when you check the snares, sitting, watching, never coming closer, never caught again.

choices.text: Take it to the fur trader in the market town

effects.log: The trader pays six taels and says red is cheap this year. On the way home you pass the dyke and every snare along it has been neatly bitten through. You never catch another hare on that dyke as long as you live.

events.text: Years after the snare on the dyke, a stranger in a plain cotton jacket helps you push your cart out of the spring mud on the market road, and walks a little way beside you, and asks, out of nowhere, whether you still set snares for hares. They limp, very slightly, on one leg.

choices.text: Say no, not since a certain morning

effects.log: "Not since a certain morning," you say. The stranger laughs, a short, surprised, barking laugh, and turns off the road into the reeds without a word of goodbye. You think you were thanked. You are almost sure you were teased.

choices.text: Look at their eyes, and say you came back to see them

effects.log: "You came back to see me," you say. The stranger stops. "You asked," they say simply. "Nobody ever asks." Then they help you with the cart all the way to the town gate, and at the gate are not there any more, and the cart is lighter than it was.

events.text: Chuseok, and the family has gone up to the hillside graves with sickles to cut the summer grass off the mounds and set out rice cakes, chestnuts and wine on the flat stone. Every year, by the time the rite is done and the family turns to go, two of the rice cakes are missing. Never more than two. This year you have been told to watch.

choices.text: Watch, and say nothing to anyone

effects.log: You watch. During the second bow, while every head is down, a red-brown paw comes out of the long grass behind the mound, takes one rice cake, and goes. Then comes back, takes another, and goes. Very neat. When you look up the family is rising from the bow, and you say nothing, and that night you sleep very well.

choices.text: Catch the thief in the act

ok.log: You grab, and you have, for one moment, a fistful of warm red fur, and then you have nothing, and a fox is sitting ten paces away on the next mound with a rice cake in its mouth, looking at you reproachfully. The family laughs until they cry. Grandfather says it has been coming since he was a boy, and leave it be.

fail.log: You lunge into the long grass and come out with burrs in your hair and a scratched cheek and nothing else. Two rice cakes are gone. Your little cousins will tell this story at every Chuseok for the rest of your life. (-3 health)

choices.text: Leave two more rice cakes, on purpose

effects.log: You set two more rice cakes behind the mound, in the long grass, where no one can see. In the morning all four are gone, and on the flat stone, very neatly, lies a sprig of red autumn leaves, the kind people put on graves in the old days. Nobody in the family can explain it but you.

events.text: It is a famine year. The family's Chuseok table on the hill is very bare: one bowl of thin rice, three chestnuts. When the rite is over and you turn to go, there are two rice cakes on the flat stone that nobody brought, still warm.

choices.text: Eat them, and bow to the long grass

effects.log: You share them out among the little ones and bow to the long grass behind the mound. Something in it shifts and is still. That winter is very hard, but your family's hens lay right through it, and nobody can say why, and you can.

choices.text: Leave them on the stone for whoever is hungrier

effects.log: You leave them. You think: it is a famine year for foxes too. In the morning they are gone. In the spring there is a hare on your doorstep, killed clean, and you understand you were not the only one being careful.

events.text: At the village school the children chant the Thousand Character Classic every morning, sky and earth, dark and yellow. This week, sitting nearest the floorboards, you have noticed something: from under the raised floor, very softly, a voice is chanting along. One beat behind. Getting better every day.

choices.text: Chant more slowly, so it can keep up

effects.log: You chant more slowly. The teacher frowns at you and then, oddly, does not correct it. By the end of the month the voice under the floor is exactly on the beat, and on the last day it says the last line alone, before anyone, in a voice like an old woman's and a child's together. The teacher puts down the switch and goes out to sit on the step for a while.

choices.text: Tell the teacher

effects.log: The teacher listens, nods, and says nothing. But that evening you see the teacher put a rice ball on the step by the gap under the floor, and the next morning it is gone, and the chanting under the floor is louder, and the teacher's eyes are very bright.

choices.text: Poke a stick under the floor

effects.log: You poke a stick under the floor. It is snatched out of your hand and does not come back. The chanting stops for three days. On the fourth day it starts again, one beat behind, and a little louder, and you feel unaccountably told off.

events.text: You are going to the county examination, and the night before, you cannot remember the order of the first lines of the Thousand Character Classic, which you have known since you were seven. You sit on the inn step in despair. From under the step, very softly, a voice begins: sky and earth, dark and yellow.

choices.text: Chant along with it until morning

effects.log: You chant along with it, line by line, all thousand characters, until the sky goes grey. At the examination your brush does not shake once. When you come back to the inn the gap under the step is empty, and smells of autumn leaves, and you bow to it before anyone is up.

choices.text: Ask it who taught it

effects.log: "Who taught you?" you whisper. A long pause. "A teacher who left rice balls," says the voice under the step, "and a child who chanted slowly." Then it goes on, sky and earth, dark and yellow, and you go on with it, and you are not afraid of anything in the morning.

events.text: You are old, and you have been asked to teach the village children their first characters, and on the first morning, as they start to chant, you hear it again from under the floor: one beat behind.

choices.text: Put a rice ball on the step tonight

effects.log: You put a rice ball on the step at dusk. It is gone at dawn. And every year that you teach, a voice under the floor learns along with the children, and every year it is a different voice, younger, and once, you are almost sure, there are two.

choices.text: Chant more slowly

effects.log: You chant more slowly, and the children, who think you are just old, slow down to match. By the end of the month the floor is on the beat. You never tell the children. One of them, a quiet one, starts leaving a rice ball on the step too, without being told.

events.text: The village has put you on the fox watch: three hens gone from the Kim family's yard in a month, and you are the one who knows a little martial art. You sit by the hen house with a lantern and a club. At the hour of the rat, two eyes come up out of the dark at the edge of the paddy, low down, catching the lantern.

choices.text: Stand up and let it see the club

roll.foeName: The fox at the hen house

ok.log: You stand up and step into the light with the club. The eyes stay where they are for a long time, considering. Then they go out, one and then the other, like a lamp being turned away. No more hens go. The Kims give you a hen of your own, which strikes you as funny.

fail.log: You stand up, trip over the lantern, set the straw by the hen house smoking, and spend the next half hour stamping out a small fire while the whole yard shrieks. When it is out, one more hen is gone. The fox did not even hurry. (-4 health)

choices.text: Sit very still and watch what it does

effects.log: You sit still. The fox comes along the dyke to the hen house, sniffs at the latch, and then, to your astonishment, goes past it to the Kims' kitchen midden and eats the fish heads and goes. You tell the Kims. They put a lock on the hen house and the fish heads outside the gate, and lose no more hens.

choices.text: Leave a hen of your own out for it

effects.log: You tie one of your own scrawny hens on a long string at the edge of the paddy. In the morning the string has been neatly untied and the hen is asleep on your roof. The Kims lose no more hens. The village thinks you are a genius. You think you were made fun of.

events.text: Some years on, still on the fox watch. This time the hens are going from a widow's yard at the edge of the village, a poor yard, and the fox comes boldly, in daylight. Its coat is thin. It is a vixen, and there are cubs somewhere.

choices.text: Give the widow two of your hens, and leave the vixen be

effects.log: You give the widow two hens and say nothing to the village. By midsummer the cubs are grown and gone and the widow's yard is left alone. One evening there is a hare on the widow's step, killed clean. She is still telling people about it.

choices.text: Find the earth and move the vixen off

ok.log: You find the earth under an old grave mound and stamp and shout until the vixen moves her cubs, one by one, across the stream to the far hill. It takes two days. Nobody is hurt. The widow's hens are safe. You feel like a landlord who has evicted a family, and are not proud of it.

fail.log: You find the earth and the vixen comes out of it at you like a red thunderbolt, and you go home bitten through the boot. The village laughs. You buy the widow two hens, sheepishly, and the fox watch is quietly given to somebody else. (-5 health)

events.text: There is a new fox at the edge of the village, and it is not taking hens. It is sitting, in broad daylight, on the dyke, watching the road, and the dogs will not go near it. The headman says it has two tails. Everyone else says the headman has been drinking.

choices.text: Walk out to the dyke and look

effects.log: You walk out along the dyke. The fox lets you come within twenty paces. It has, when it turns its head, very clearly, two tails. It looks at you as a person looks at a person. Then it gets up and goes along the dyke toward the hills, unhurried, and you stand there with your heart going hard. You tell the headman he was not drinking. He looks very relieved.

choices.text: Keep the dogs in and leave it alone

effects.log: You keep the dogs in. The fox sits on the dyke three days, watching the road, and on the fourth day a pale traveller in a good jacket comes down the road and the fox gets up and is gone, and the traveller stays at the wine-house two nights and asks a great many questions about the village. Nobody connects the two things but you.

events.text: On the road into the village you fall in beside a salt peddler with an A-frame of salt on his back and a forked stick in his hand. Ahead of you an old woman is walking into the village in a round hat that is not quite the shape of any hat you know. The salt peddler is watching her the way a cat watches a hole. "Look at the hat," he says, very low. "Then look at the shadow."

choices.text: Look at the shadow

effects.log: You look. The old woman's shadow on the bright road has a tail. Just one, long and brushed. You look up and she is turning in at the gate of a house with a young scholar in it. The salt peddler grunts, as if you had passed a test. "Fire sees what earth hides," he says. "That is why they hate us."

choices.text: Say: leave the old woman alone

effects.log: "Leave her alone," you say. The salt peddler looks at you with interest. "If she is an old woman," he says, "she will not mind a salt peddler walking behind her. If she is not, she will." You walk behind her together. At the gate she turns, and sees the salt peddler, and her face slips, very slightly, like a mask on a string, and she is gone into the reeds.

choices.text: Ask what the stick is for

effects.log: "Holding up the A-frame," says the salt peddler, "when I rest. And for other things." He shows you: an ordinary forked stick, worn smooth. "Wood beats earth," he says. "An old foolish rule. It works." Ahead of you the old woman in the hat has heard, and is walking much faster.

events.text: The salt peddler is in the village again, years older, and this time he is waiting at the gate of the house where the old woman in the hat went in. He has his stick. The young scholar of the house is grown, and pale, and the old woman, they say, has lived with the family all this while, as an old nurse.

choices.text: Stand with the salt peddler

roll.foeName: The old nurse in the hat

ok.log: The old nurse comes to the gate and sees the stick, and the face slips, and for one moment you see the whole thing, the long muzzle, the eyes, four tails like a fan of smoke, and then the salt peddler's stick cracks down on the gatepost between you and it, and it is gone over the wall. The scholar of the house recovers in a month. The salt peddler buys you a bowl of soup and says nothing else.

fail.log: The old nurse comes to the gate and something hits you like a wind full of claws, and you go over backwards. When you get up the salt peddler is sitting in the road with his stick broken, laughing, and the old nurse is gone, and the scholar of the house is sitting up in bed asking for rice. "Well," says the salt peddler. "That worked anyway." (-8 health)

choices.text: Go in first and speak to the old nurse

effects.log: You go in and find the old nurse by the scholar's bed, and sit down at the other end of the room, and say that there is a salt peddler at the gate. The old nurse looks at you, and at the sleeping scholar, a long time. "All these years," the nurse says. "Tell him I am going." And is gone, by the back way, and the scholar wakes up and asks for rice.

choices.text: Walk on: it is not your house

effects.log: You walk on. You hear later that the salt peddler stood at the gate all day, and at dusk the old nurse came out, looked at him, and walked off up the hill without a word, and the scholar of the house got better, and the salt peddler bought himself a jar of wine with nobody's money but his own.

events.text: The salt peddler's grandson, a gentle young person with the same forked stick, comes to find you. "My grandfather spoke of you," they say. "He chased foxes all his life. I have chased one. It sat down in the road and asked me why my grandfather hated them. I did not know. I thought you might."

choices.text: Tell them: he did not hate them; he was afraid for the scholars

effects.log: "He did not hate them," you say. "He was afraid for the people they drank from. He was a salt peddler. He walked every road and saw every pale student." The grandchild thinks about that. "Then I can keep the stick," they say slowly, "and not hate them." They go away looking much lighter.

choices.text: Say: ask the fox; it knows more than I do

effects.log: "Ask the fox," you say. They stare. They go. A year later a letter comes: they asked. They sat in the road and talked with it until dawn. They still carry the stick, they write, and they have not used it since, and they buy their salt from a quiet old seller at the crossroads who will not say how old she is.

events.text: Your sect elder has sent you to the market town with a purse to buy "fox bead" from an old apothecary: a famous medicine, the elder says, ground from a shell, good for coughs. The apothecary looks at you a long time, goes to the back, and comes out with a small box. Inside is not a shell. It is a pale bead the size of a pea, and it is warm, and it is glowing, faintly, in the dark of the shop.

choices.text: Ask where it came from

effects.log: "A fox came to my back door twenty years ago," the apothecary says, "with a sick child in a sling, a human child, and left this with me for the medicine. I have never dared sell it. Your elder's order is the first that asked by name." The bead pulses in its box, slow as a heart.

choices.text: Buy it, as ordered

effects.log: You pay eight taels and carry it home in your sleeve, warm against your arm all the way. Your elder opens the box, goes white, closes it, and takes you aside. "That is not cough medicine," the elder says. "Somebody wants this back. Somebody very old."

choices.text: Refuse to buy it: it is not a shell

effects.log: "This is not what I was sent for," you say, and hand the box back. The apothecary looks relieved almost to tears. Going home empty-handed, you are scolded by your elder, and you do not mind, because all the way home a fox has been walking along the ridge above the road, keeping pace with you, and at the sect gate it sits down and bows.

events.text: Somebody has come for the bead. At the apothecary's back door, in the rain, a thin person in a wet cotton jacket is standing, asking very politely to have back what they left for a child twenty years ago. The child, they say, is grown. They need it now. The apothecary has sent for you.

choices.text: Give it back to them

effects.log: You put the bead in their open palm. They close their fingers on it and their face, for one breath, is not a human face at all, but a tired, narrow, red-brown face with eyes full of rain. "Thank you," they say. "I have been very cold." In the morning there is a jar of good honey on the apothecary's step, and a second on yours.

choices.text: Ask them first why they need it

effects.log: "Because I have been living without it twenty years," they say, "and I am getting old the way you do, and I do not know how." You give it back. They hold it a moment, and then press it, briefly, to the apothecary's forehead, and the old apothecary's cough, which has gone on for years, stops. Then they are gone.

events.text: There is a matchmaker in the county whose matches never fail. Thirty years, a hundred houses, not one unhappy pair. The other matchmakers are furious, and one of them has paid you to find out how it is done. You watch the matchmaker's house for a week. Every evening, the lamp casts the matchmaker's shadow on the paper door, and the shadow has a tail.
events.arc: The Matchmaker of a Hundred Houses

choices.text: Report the truth to the one who paid you

effects.log: You report it. The other matchmaker goes pale, and then thoughtful, and then does nothing whatever with it. "If I say a fox matched them," the rival says, "a hundred happy houses will start wondering. I am not a monster." You keep the fee anyway.

choices.text: Knock on the matchmaker's door and ask how it is done

effects.log: The matchmaker lets you in, pours tea, and answers without a blink. "I can smell when two people are lonely in the same way," the matchmaker says. "It is a small trick. Foxes are very lonely animals." A pause. "Your employer is lonely in your way, too, by the way. Shall I?"

choices.text: Return the fee and say nothing

effects.log: You give back the money and say you found nothing. The rival matchmaker is suspicious but helpless. A month later a red-wrapped parcel arrives at your own door, from the matchmaker of the hundred houses, unasked, with a note: no obligation; a thank-you. Inside is a caddy of the best tea in the county. You drink it slowly, over a year.

events.text: The matchmaker of a hundred houses is leaving the county: too many people have noticed that the matchmaker has not aged in all these years. On the last night there is a gathering at the house, all the couples of a hundred matches, old and young, drinking to the one who matched them, and you are invited.
events.arc: The Matchmaker of a Hundred Houses

choices.text: Go, and raise a cup

effects.log: You go and raise a cup with a hundred happy houses. At the end of the night the matchmaker comes and sits by you. "Not one of them knows," says the matchmaker. "Not one of them needs to." In the morning the house is empty and swept, and on the step is a bundle of red thread.

choices.text: Stay away, and let them say goodbye without you

effects.log: You stay away. It is their night. But from your window you hear the singing go on till dawn, and at dawn, on the road out of the county, a figure walking alone with a small bundle, and a red-brown tail very plainly showing under the hem of the jacket, which, for once, it is not bothering to hide.

events.text: A governor's bounty on a fox that has been taking breath from students at the county school, and you have been hired to go with {npc}, the best fox hunter in three provinces, who brings two yellow dogs and a falcon and very few words. In the first snow on the hill of graves the tracks are clear. {npc} studies them a long time. "Two foxes," {npc} says. "One is the one we want. One is following it, to stop it."
events.arc: The Best Hunter in Three Provinces

choices.text: Go after the first one, as hired

roll.foeName: The fox of the school road

ok.log: You run it down at the edge of the pines, a lean dark fox with three tails that turns at bay and spits foxfire at you, and you go through the fire and drive it off the hill and over the river, out of the province, with {npc}'s falcon screaming overhead. You do not kill it. {npc} does not ask you to. The county school's students get their colour back by spring.

fail.log: You run it down at the edge of the pines and it turns and spits foxfire in your face and you are on your back in the snow, blind for an hour. When you can see again, {npc} is sitting beside you and the tracks of both foxes go off over the river together, side by side. "The second one took it away," {npc} says. "Good enough." (-10 health)

choices.text: Follow the second set of tracks instead

effects.log: You follow the second set, with {npc} grumbling behind you, and at the top of the hill you find a small red vixen sitting in the snow over the first fox, which is asleep, or something like asleep, with its tails over its nose. The vixen looks up at you. "I will take it away," it says, in a voice like a girl's. "Over the river. It will not come back." {npc} lowers the bow. "In all my years," {npc} says afterwards, "no fox ever spoke to me."

choices.text: Ask {npc} why {he} hunts foxes

effects.log: {npc} is silent a long time, scraping snow off the dogs' feet. "A student in my village," {npc} says at last. "My friend. Pale, all one autumn. The schoolmaster told my friend the story too late." A pause. "I do not hate them. I hunt the ones that drink. The others I let go." You hunt together all that week and drive the fox of the school road out of the province without killing it.

events.text: {npc}, the fox hunter, has sent for you. A governor wants a white fox for the collar of a winter coat, and has offered {npc} more money than {npc} has seen in a lifetime. "I have found one," {npc} says. "White, five tails, lives as a herb physician in the next valley. Has never drunk from anyone in my hearing. I want you to tell me to say no."
events.arc: The Best Hunter in Three Provinces

choices.text: Tell {npc} to say no

effects.log: "Say no," you say. {npc} breathes out like someone putting down a heavy load. {npc} writes to the governor that the white fox could not be found, and goes and buys medicine for {his} old dog from the herb physician in the next valley, and pays double.

choices.text: Say it is {npc}'s choice, not yours

effects.log: "It is your choice," you say. {npc} nods slowly. In the end {npc} says no anyway, and gives up hunting that winter, and sells the falcon, and keeps the dogs. "I wanted someone to tell me," {npc} says, the last time you see {him}. "Nobody ever does. So I had to."

events.text: {npc} the old fox hunter has died, and left you the two yellow dogs, both grey-muzzled now, and a letter. The letter says: when I am buried, take the dogs up the hill of graves once more, and let them off the rope.
events.arc: The Best Hunter in Three Provinces

choices.text: Take them up and let them go

effects.npcPass: old age, with two old dogs at the gate
effects.log: You let them off the rope at the top of the hill. They do not chase anything. They go and lie down, both of them, at the foot of an old grave mound, wagging, and something in the dark mouth of the earth under it is wagging too, a red-brown tail. You leave the dogs there till dusk. They come home on their own, very pleased.

choices.text: Keep them by you; the hill can wait

effects.npcPass: old age, with two old dogs at the gate
effects.log: You keep them by you. They are good old dogs. But every evening they stand at the gate and look toward the hill of graves, and on the evening the second one dies, there is a fox sitting on the hill road looking back, quite still, as if paying a call.

events.text: In the poor quarter of the provincial town there is a herb physician, {npc}, who cures what no one else can: fevers that have gone on all summer, coughs from the mines, children nobody expected to live. {npc} sees patients only by daylight. At dusk the shutters go up and the door is barred, and no one has ever seen {npc} by lamplight. Your own old wound, the one from the bandit's spear, has been hurting for a year, and {npc} is your last hope.

choices.text: Go by daylight, like everyone

effects.log: You wait half a day in the queue with the miners and the mothers. {npc} looks at your old wound for a long moment, presses two fingers to it, and something warm goes through it like spring water through ice. "Come back in a month," {npc} says, not looking up. You go home, and for the first time in a year sleep through the night. (+15 health)

choices.text: Go after dark, when no one is watching

effects.log: You knock at the barred door after dark. A long silence. Then the door opens a crack and {npc} looks out at you in the lamplight, and the eyes catch it like a cat's, and behind {him}, on the wall, the shadow has three tails. "You had better come in, then," {npc} says, very tired. {npc} treats your wound by the light of a single shielded candle and says nothing about the shadow, and neither do you. (+10 health)

choices.text: Watch the clinic first: something is wrong here

effects.log: You watch for three days. You see {npc} turn no one away, take payment in eggs and turnips, and once, very late, carry a sleeping child home through the dark to a house in the next street, and come back at a run. You go in on the fourth day, by daylight, and your old wound is healed in a month, and you are ashamed of the three days.

events.text: A master from a righteous sect has come to the provincial town to kill a fox. Someone has told the sect that the herb physician {npc} is a fox spirit. The master is at the clinic gate now, with a sword, and the waiting room is full of the poor.

choices.text: Stand in the gateway between them

ok.log: You stand in the gateway. The master tries you, once, twice, and the third time stops, with the point of the sword a hand from your throat, and looks past you at the waiting room: a miner with a cough, a mother with a child, an old soldier with no feet. "These are what it does?" the master asks. "These are what {npc} does," you say. The master sheathes the sword and joins the queue, and is seen to by daylight, for a bad knee.

fail.log: You stand in the gateway and the master goes through you like wind through grass, and you are on the stones bleeding. But it took long enough. When the master gets to the back room {npc} is gone, by the window, and the waiting room of the poor has closed round the gate like a wall and will not let the master out until the sect elder is sent for. (-14 health)

choices.text: Tell the master to wait in the queue and see

effects.log: "Wait in the queue," you say. "See what it does. Then kill it, if you still want to." The master, who is not a fool, waits. It takes all day. By evening the master has watched {npc} save two children and a miner, and goes out of the gate without a word, and leaves the sword's tassel tied to the gatepost, which in that sect means: under my protection.

choices.text: Run in and warn {npc} to go by the back

effects.log: You run in by the side door. {npc} hears you, and puts down a bowl of medicine, and finishes giving it to the child first, every drop. Then {npc} goes out of the back window like smoke. The town loses its physician. You hear, a year later, of a herb physician three provinces away who sees patients only by daylight.

events.text: A letter in a physician's neat hand, from {npc}, years after the clinic: "I am trying a long thing, a thousand days without harm. I am on day nine hundred and forty. There is a child in this town with a fever I could cure with my breath in a night, and it would break the count, because of how it is done. Tell me what a human would do."

choices.text: Write back: cure the child, and start the count again

effects.log: You write it, and send it, and do not sleep for a week. A second letter comes in the spring. "The child is well. I am on day one hundred and four. I am not sorry. Thank you for saying it, so that I did not have to say it alone."

choices.text: Write back: there must be another way; look for it

effects.log: You write it. A second letter comes in the spring. "There was another way. A slower medicine, every hour for six days, by hand. I did not sleep. The child is well. I am on day one thousand and six." At the bottom, in a hand that wobbles: "Day one thousand was very quiet. I wanted to tell someone."

events.text: A plague year, and the physicians of the province are dying faster than the sick. In the worst quarter of the town, a herb physician no one knows has opened a clinic, and keeps it open by lamplight, all night, every night, with the shutters wide. In the lamplight, on the wall behind, there is a shadow with many tails, and nobody in that quarter cares at all.

choices.text: Go and work beside the physician

effects.log: You carry water and boil cloths and hold the dying by lamplight for forty nights beside a physician who does not hide any more. Nobody in the quarter says the word fox. When the plague breaks the physician is gone one morning, and the quarter builds a small shrine with no name on it, and keeps a lamp lit in it. (-8 health)

choices.text: Bring the town's grain stores to that quarter

ok.log: You shout and bully and promise until the magistrate opens the grain store to that quarter. Fed people live. The physician, the one night you come by, looks at the sacks of grain, and at you, and bows very low, and the shadow on the wall bows too.

fail.log: The magistrate will not open the store. You carry what you can on your own back. It is not enough. It is not nothing either, the physician tells you, in the grey before dawn, and you both go on.

events.text: The geomancer everyone in the province wants is a quiet person in a grey robe who has never chosen a bad site: not a grave, not a well, not a house. Your sect wants a new hall and has sent you to escort the geomancer over the ridges. The geomancer walks without looking at the compass, touches the earth now and then with two fingers, and will not say how it is done.
events.arc: The Geomancer Who Would Not Say

choices.text: Watch how it is done

effects.log: You watch. The geomancer stops where the grass is a different green, kneels, and breathes in, long and slow, over the earth, and the breath that comes out is faintly silver in the cold.
