You do not say anything. The geomancer looks up at you and says, mildly: "Everyone breathes. I only listen to what comes back."

choices.text: Ask straight out

effects.log: "How?" you ask. The geomancer smiles. "I lived a long time in a graveyard," comes the answer. "Graves teach you where the earth is cold and where it is warm. Most people do not stay long enough." The site chosen for your sect's hall is very good. The sect has had nothing but luck since.

choices.text: Test it: bury a coin and ask where

effects.log: You bury a coin by night under a pine. In the morning you ask, casually, whether the ridge holds any metal. The geomancer walks straight to the pine, looks at you with eyes that catch the sun, and says: "Only one coin. And yours." You are both quiet the rest of the way.

events.text: Two great families are at law over the same hillside: both claim a grave site there, both have a geomancer's word that it is the best in the province, and the magistrate has asked the quiet geomancer in grey to settle it. The geomancer has asked for you, as a witness nobody can bribe.
events.arc: The Geomancer Who Would Not Say

choices.text: Stand as witness, and say exactly what you see

effects.log: The geomancer walks the hill and says: the site is good, but it is good because of an old grave already on it, nameless, very old, a mound nobody tends. "Move that one," the geomancer says, "and the site is nothing." Both families withdraw. The geomancer, on the way down, cuts the grass on the nameless mound, very carefully. You help.

choices.text: Ask the geomancer, privately, whose grave it is

effects.log: "My mother's," says the geomancer, after a long pause. "She was a fox of this hill. It is the best earth in the province because she lay in it a long time." Then, in court, the geomancer says only that the site cannot be used. Both families accept it. You never repeat what you were told.

events.text: A royal order: the court wants the quiet geomancer in grey to choose a king's tomb, and the geomancer has vanished. You are sent to find them. You know where to look. You find the geomancer on the hill of the nameless mound, sitting in the grass, with the royal letter unopened beside them.
events.arc: The Geomancer Who Would Not Say

choices.text: Say you could not find them

effects.log: You go back and report that the geomancer could not be found. The court chooses another, and the king's tomb is good enough. Years later, passing that hill, you see grey cloth fluttering on the nameless mound, tied there like a prayer strip, and the grass cut.

choices.text: Ask them to go: a king's tomb chosen badly harms a kingdom

effects.log: The geomancer listens, and sighs, and goes. The tomb is chosen perfectly. At court the geomancer is offered rank and refuses it, and is seen in the palace only by daylight, and is gone, quietly, before the year is out. The kingdom has a long, quiet reign. Nobody ever knows why but you.

events.text: A young Taoist trickster of the Jeon clan has fallen in with you on the road: clever, loud, and very interested in foxes. "The old books say a fox's bead swallowed gives a person seventy-two transformations," the trickster says. "I know where one drinks: at the mountain temple, at dusk, from the wine the monks leave for the gods. You are strong. I am clever. Shall we?"
events.arc: The Trickster of the Jeon Clan

choices.text: Go along, to keep the trickster from doing anything foolish

effects.log: At dusk at the temple a fox comes out of the trees and drinks the offering wine until it sways. The trickster leaps out with a rope and ties it up, laughing. The fox, very drunk, offers a book for its freedom. The trickster looks at you. You look at the fox, and at the rope. "Let it go," you say. Grumbling, the trickster takes the book and lets it go. The book, when opened, turns out to be blank.

choices.text: Refuse, and warn the temple monks

effects.log: You warn the monks. That evening there is no wine on the altar, only tea, and the trickster, crouched in the bushes all night with a rope, catches nothing but cold. In the morning a fox sits on the temple wall looking down at the trickster with what you could swear is pity.

choices.text: Go along, and try to take the bead yourself

ok.log: At dusk you are quicker than the trickster: you have the fox by the scruff before it is half drunk. It goes very still. Then it opens its mouth and says, in a scholar's voice, "Look at me," and you do, and you are sitting in the temple courtyard alone at dawn with a headache and an empty offering bowl in your lap. The trickster is laughing so hard he has to lie down.

fail.log: You grab and miss and land face first in the offering wine. The fox, not drunk at all, sits on the altar and watches you crawl out. The trickster is laughing so hard he has to lie down. You smell of temple wine for a week. (-6 health)

events.text: The trickster of the Jeon clan is famous now, and in trouble: he swallowed a fox's bead in the end, from some other fox on some other road, and now has seventy-two shapes and the whole court hunting him for mocking a minister. He has come to you as a crow, a cat, and finally himself, thin and frightened. "I want to give it back," he says. "I do not know how."
events.arc: The Trickster of the Jeon Clan

choices.text: Take him to the temple at dusk and wait for the fox

effects.log: You sit together in the temple courtyard at dusk with a jar of wine on the altar. A fox comes, old and grey, and sits on the wall and looks at the trickster. The trickster opens his mouth and the bead comes out, all on its own, a little dim, and floats across the courtyard into the fox's mouth. The trickster weeps. The fox, you think, also does, a little. Then they both go their ways.

choices.text: Tell him to use it well instead, for the poor

effects.log: "You cannot give back a swallowed thing," you say. "Use it for the people the minister robs." He does, after a fashion, wildly, with a great many jokes, for years. The villages love him. The foxes, you hear, rather like him too.

events.text: The province was saved from famine three years ago by one piece of advice: a palace attendant who told the governor to open the granaries a month before anyone else saw the drought coming. You have been made the governor's guard captain, and tonight, walking the corridor, you see that attendant's shadow on a lit paper screen, writing at a desk. The shadow has six tails.

choices.text: Walk on and say nothing

effects.log: You walk on. Your footsteps do not change. Behind you the shadow on the screen goes very still, and then, slowly, goes on writing. In the morning the attendant passes you in the courtyard and gives you the smallest nod in the world. You give one back.

choices.text: Knock and go in

effects.log: You knock. A long pause. "Come in," says the attendant, and you do, and the room is ordinary and the shadow is ordinary, and the attendant is very pale. "I saw," you say. The attendant puts down the brush. "Then you know what I am. Do you know what I have done here?" You do: the granaries, three years of good advice, not one breath taken. "I know that too," you say.

choices.text: Report it to the governor

effects.log: You report it. The governor listens with a face like stone and says: "I know. Who do you think told me about the drought?" A pause. "Forget you said it. I already have." You go away feeling extremely young.

events.text: A minister from the capital has come to the province with a monk who carries a bell, and they are asking about the palace attendant with good advice. The monk's bell rings by itself in the attendant's corridor. The minister suspects, and is right, and has come to you, the guard captain, for a key.

choices.text: Give the minister the wrong key

effects.log: You give the minister the key to the linen store. By the time the mistake is found, the attendant's room is empty and swept, and on the desk is a last memorandum to the governor, about next year's rice, and it is very good advice.

choices.text: Ask the minister what the attendant has done wrong

effects.log: The minister is quiet a long time. "Nothing," the minister says at last. "I have read every order this province sent for five years. Nothing at all." The minister sends the monk home, and goes, and keeps it to themself for the rest of their career, and you think that is the bravest thing you have seen a minister do.

choices.text: Stand at the attendant's door yourself

ok.log: You stand at the door. The monk rings the bell at you, and it is only a bell. The minister looks at you a long time, and then at the door, and goes away. The attendant leaves the province anyway, a month later, of their own accord, and leaves you a letter that you keep in your sleeve for years.

fail.log: The monk's bell rings and rings, and something in the ringing knocks you to your knees, and the minister walks past you into the room. It is empty. The window is open, and the night is full of the smell of autumn leaves. (-8 health)

events.text: Years later you are in the capital, and a court physician walks past you in a palace corridor in a dark official robe, and stops, and turns. Different face. Same nod.

choices.text: Nod back

effects.log: You nod back. The court physician walks on. That year the court passes a famine law that opens granaries a month early, every year, by rule. Nobody remembers who proposed it. You do.

choices.text: Follow, and ask for a cup of tea

effects.log: Over tea in a small dark office, the court physician says: "A king's ear is a terrible thing to have. I try to use it for rice and nothing else. It is harder than you would think." Then, more quietly: "Thank you for the key."

choices.text: Warn them that the capital has more bells

effects.log: "The capital has more bells," you say. The physician smiles. "I know. I have been here twelve years." Then, after a moment: "Thank you. Nobody has ever warned me before. I did not know it would feel like this."

events.text: A rumour at court: there is a fox in the palace whispering to the king, and the old ministers want a purge of every servant who came from the provinces. Your name is on the list of those to carry it out.

choices.text: Refuse to carry it out

effects.log: You refuse, in writing, and are sent back to your province in disgrace. The purge goes ahead without you, and catches forty servants, every one of them human. The fox, if there was one, is not among them. You hear the old ministers grumbled about that for years.

choices.text: Carry it out slowly, and lose the list

effects.log: You carry it out so slowly and so thoroughly, with so many hearings and so many witnesses, that the old ministers lose interest by the autumn, and the list, somehow, is lost in a flood in the records office. Nobody is purged. You are thought a very dull official. Good.

events.text: The governor of the northern province wants a white fox for the collar of a winter coat, and has heard that you are the strongest martial artist within ten days' ride. The fee is enormous. "There is one on Pine Ridge," the governor says. "Many tails. White as a mourning robe. The hunters cannot catch it. Bring it in."

choices.text: Take the job, and go and look

effects.log: You take the governor's silver and go up Pine Ridge in the first snow. You find the tracks easily. Too easily. They lead in a great slow circle, all day, round and round the ridge, and at dusk you find yourself exactly where you started, with a small pile of pine cones on your pack that you did not put there.

choices.text: Refuse

effects.log: You refuse. The governor is not used to being refused, and makes your life difficult for a year. You do not mind. The white fox of Pine Ridge is not caught that winter, or the next, and the governor, you hear, wears sable, and complains.

choices.text: Take the money and warn the fox

effects.log: You take twenty taels of silver and climb Pine Ridge and shout into the snow that a governor wants a collar and the hunters of three counties are coming. You feel ridiculous. In the morning there is a line of white tracks going north over the pass, out of the province. You report failure. You keep the silver, and are not sure you deserve to.

events.text: On Pine Ridge again, in the deep snow, you find the white fox at last: caught, by the hunters of three counties, in a trap baited with the scent of another fox. It is very old and very white. It is not struggling. Five hunters with spears are coming up the ridge to finish it, and the governor's silver is still in your sleeve.

choices.text: Open the trap

effects.log: You open the trap. The white fox gets up, slowly, on a hurt leg, and looks at you with eyes the colour of a winter sky, and goes away north over the snow. The hunters arrive and stand there looking at the empty trap and at you. Nobody says anything. You give the governor back the silver and leave the province.

choices.text: Stand between the hunters and the trap

ok.log: Five spears, and you take them one by one and break them over your knee, and nobody is hurt but their pride. While you argue with the hunters the white fox gets its leg out of the trap and is gone. The governor wears sable.

fail.log: Five spears is a great many. You go down in the snow. But while you were fighting, the white fox chewed through the trap's cord and was gone, and the hunters, standing over you, look at the empty trap and spit, and carry you down the ridge. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let the hunters come

effects.log: You stand aside. The hunters come. You do not watch. The governor pays you thirty taels and wears the collar all that winter. You see it once, at a feast, white as a mourning robe, and you have to leave the room.

events.text: The governor who wanted the white collar has fallen from favour and is dying in exile, poor, in a cold room. He has asked for you. "I wanted something no one else had," he says. "That is all it was. Something white."

choices.text: Sit with him

effects.log: You sit with him through a long night. He talks about his mother, and about the snow when he was a boy. At dawn, through the window, you both see it: a white fox on the far ridge, sitting quite still, looking at the house. The governor weeps. Then he sleeps, and does not wake.

choices.text: Tell him plainly what the collar would have cost

effects.log: You tell him: a very old animal that had harmed no one, for a coat that would be moth-eaten in a few years. He listens. "Yes," he says. "Yes. I know." It is the most honest thing he has ever said, and it is too late, and you are glad anyway that he said it.

events.text: An alchemist of great reputation wants to hire you. The elixir of a thousand years, the alchemist says, needs one thing no one has ever brought: the bead of a nine-tailed fox. "Not killed," the alchemist adds quickly. "I am not a butcher. Taken. You are strong enough to take it."
events.arc: The Elixir of a Thousand Years

choices.text: Ask whether the fox can live without it

effects.log: The alchemist hesitates too long. "It would be an ordinary fox again," the alchemist says. "With nine tails' worth of memory and nothing else. It would probably die of grief in a ditch." You decline. The alchemist is genuinely surprised that anyone would.

choices.text: Refuse outright

effects.log: You refuse. The alchemist shrugs and hires someone else. Three months later the someone else comes back, without the bead, very quiet, and takes up farming, and will not talk about it to anyone.

choices.text: Take the job, meaning to fail

effects.log: You take fifteen taels and spend a season wandering the mountains looking, very carefully, in all the wrong places. Once, at the top of a ridge, you see foxfire on the next ridge, nine points of it, fanning out, and you turn and walk the other way. You tell the alchemist there are no such foxes. You lie well.

events.text: The alchemist has made the elixir anyway, with a bead bought from a stranger at a night market, and drunk it, and now sits in the workshop seeing every vein of water under the province and every grave and every buried coin, and cannot stop seeing them, and cannot sleep. "I wanted the sky," the alchemist says. "I got the earth."
events.arc: The Elixir of a Thousand Years

choices.text: Sit with the alchemist and tell the old story

effects.log: You tell the old story: the student, the bead, look at the sky, the fall, the earth. The alchemist laughs till it turns into crying. "Everyone who swallows it looks down," the alchemist says. "Of course they do. We are people." Some months later the alchemist is a geomancer of some fame, and sleeps a little.

choices.text: Find the stranger who sold the bead

effects.log: You search the night market for a month. On the last night a pedlar of old jars tells you, unasked, that the stranger was a fox selling a dead fox's bead, to give it to someone who would use it instead of letting it rot. "Foxes are practical," says the pedlar, and when you look again the stall is gone.

events.text: You have been made second to {npc}, the general the villages call fox-born: a foundling found at a grave mound, they say, raised by a widowed herb-seller nobody ever saw by lamplight, and so quick that at twelve {he} caught a tiger cub with bare hands. {npc} is quiet, very good, and has one standing order nobody understands: the army never hunts, camps, or forages on one particular hill.

choices.text: Obey the order without asking

effects.log: You obey it. You make the quartermasters obey it. In three years nobody sets foot on that hill. {npc} notices. One evening, without a word, {npc} pours you a cup of tea from the officers' own pot, and you understand you have passed something that was never called a test.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why

effects.log: {npc} looks at the hill a long time. "Someone I owe everything to lives there," {npc} says. "Or is buried there. I am not sure which. Either way it is theirs." Then, after a long pause: "They used to tell me not to listen to what the villages said. I did not, until I was grown. Then I listened, and it was true, and it did not matter."

choices.text: Walk up the hill alone one evening and look

effects.log: You go up at dusk. At the top, by an old grave mound, an elderly fox with a grey muzzle is lying in the last of the sun, watching the camp below with its chin on its paws. It sees you. It does not get up. You sit down at a polite distance, and the two of you watch {npc}'s tent until the lamps are lit. You say nothing about it to anyone.

events.text: The court has ordered {npc}, the fox-born general, to lead a great fox hunt: a nine-tailed fox is said to be draining students in the south. {npc} has accepted, and has drawn the hunting map, and you see that the map goes round the one hill without touching it, like water round a stone.

choices.text: Say nothing about the hill, and ride

roll.foeName: The nine-tailed fox of the south

ok.log: You ride with {npc}, and the hunt is real: a dark fox with nine tails of cold foxfire, at bay in a gorge, and {npc} goes in first, quick as nobody should be, and drives it off a cliff into the sea mist. It is not seen again. The southern students recover. Coming home, the army goes round the one hill without being told.

fail.log: You ride with {npc}, and in the gorge the dark fox's foxfire takes you full in the chest and you go down. {npc} stands over you until it is driven off. You wake in a farmhouse at the foot of a quiet hill, bandaged, with a bowl of herb broth beside you that nobody in the farmhouse made. (-12 health)

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether the hunt is just

effects.log: "The southern fox drinks students," {npc} says. "Mine never did. A fox is not one thing any more than a soldier is." {npc} leads the hunt, and it is short and clean, and the army goes round the hill. You think {npc} is the only general in the kingdom who could have told the difference.

events.text: {npc} has come back from the wars for the last time, grey, and has asked you to ride out with {him} to the quiet hill. At the top there is a small grave mound, newly raised, the grass not yet grown on it. "I found it lying here last spring," {npc} says. "Very old. Grey in the muzzle. On the slope above my house, where it could see the roof."

choices.text: Help {npc} cut the grass and set out the rite

effects.log: You cut the grass, and set out rice, chestnuts and a cup of wine on a flat stone, and {npc} bows, twice, as to a parent. Nobody will ever know who lies here. {npc} does. That is enough, {npc} says, and you believe it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether {he} ever knew for certain

effects.log: {npc} smiles. "A herb-seller who never ate meat and never slept by lamplight, who could find any child lost in the hills, and who smelled, always, of autumn leaves," {npc} says. "I knew when I was seven. I pretended not to for years, because it seemed to matter to them that I did not."

events.text: A young soldier in your own command has a nickname the others use behind their back: fox-born. Found at a grave mound, raised by nobody knows whom, very quick. Today the others have set dogs on the soldier's tent for a joke.

choices.text: Put a stop to it, hard

effects.log: You put a stop to it, in front of the whole company. Afterwards you tell the young soldier about a general you once served, who went round a hill. The soldier listens with eyes very wide, and says nothing, and never forgets.

choices.text: Make the young soldier your runner

effects.log: You make the soldier your runner, which puts a stop to it without a word. The soldier is the best runner you ever had, and finds every lost patrol in the hills, and at night, in camp, the dogs come and lie down at the runner's feet.

events.text: A thousand-year fox has drained a girl in a mountain village, not to death, but near it; the village has begged you, and you have hunted it for a month, and tonight, with talisman ropes and all your art, you have it bound in a clearing by an old grave. It is white, and very old, and lies quite still in the ropes. "Before you kill me," it says, "will you listen to me, for one night?"
events.arc: A Fox Bound by an Old Grave

choices.text: Listen

effects.log: You listen all night. It tells you about a voice from heaven a thousand years ago, and a poem it was promised, and ten years of waiting at a grave, hungry, and a girl whose breath was warm, and how it stopped. It does not ask to be forgiven. At dawn you loosen the ropes. "Go," you say. It goes, slowly, looking back once, and the girl in the village wakes up asking for rice.

choices.text: Listen, and then give it the poem it wants

ok.log: When it has told you everything, you write it a poem, there in the clearing by moonlight: smoke round a lonely grave, a mottled pelt laid down like an old robe. It reads the poem with its eyes wet. You loosen the ropes. It walks away out of the clearing and, at the edge of the trees, it is walking on two feet, and then it is gone.

fail.log: When it has told you everything, you try to write it a poem, and it will not come. You are a fighter, not a poet. The fox watches you struggle with something like kindness. "It must be given freely and well," it says. "You gave freely. That is half." You let it go anyway.

choices.text: Kill it, as the village asked

ok.log: You do not listen. You end it quickly, as cleanly as you can, and carry word back down to the village. The girl recovers. You are paid and praised. And for the rest of your life, now and then, you find yourself wondering what it would have said.

fail.log: It breaks the ropes the moment you raise your hand, as if it had been allowed to be bound, and is gone into the mist. You hear it, far off, laughing, or crying. The girl recovers anyway. You never find it again. (-10 health)

events.text: Years after the clearing by the old grave, a person you have never seen comes to your gate, perfectly ordinary, with tired brown eyes and grey in their hair, carrying a jar of wine. "You listened," they say. "Nobody had, in a thousand years. I am getting old now. It is very strange. I wanted to show you."
events.arc: A Fox Bound by an Old Grave

choices.text: Invite them in and put the kettle on

effects.log: You sit together on the porch with a pot of tea until dark. They tell you about aching knees and cold mornings and a neighbour's child they are teaching to read, and they are happier than anyone you have ever met. When they go, their shadow on the gate, in the lamplight, is perfectly ordinary.

choices.text: Ask whether it was worth it

effects.log: "Ask me when I am dying," they say, and laugh. "I think so. I cannot see in the dark any more. I am cold. Everyone I meet will be dead before I get to know them properly, and I them. It is wonderful." You do not understand, and then, slowly, you do.

events.text: A young martial artist has come to ask your advice: they have a fox bound in talisman ropes in the hills, very old, and it has asked them to listen for one night before they kill it.
events.arc: A Fox Bound by an Old Grave

choices.text: Tell them to listen

effects.log: "Listen," you say. "Then decide. You will decide better." They go. They come back a week later, and sit down on your step without asking, and are quiet for a long time, and then they say: "I let it go." You pour them tea. That is all the advice there ever is.

choices.text: Tell them about your own night by the grave

effects.log: You tell them about the clearing, and the jar of wine years later, and the ordinary shadow on your gate. They listen, and go back to the hills, and you never learn what they decided. You think you know.

events.text: Three villages on the mountain have been praying for years to a mountain goddess who answers every prayer, and the old woman who used to keep the goddess's shrine has been seen sleeping in a woodcutter's hut. Now the sky over the ridge is going black, and you, the strongest master in the province, feel three great forces coming down it: wind, rain and lightning, sent from above, for whoever sits in that shrine.

choices.text: Go up and stand at the shrine gate

ok.log: You stand at the gate in the storm. The wind comes first and you turn it, and the rain and you part it, and the lightning stops a pace from your face and waits, and a voice in it says, quite reasonably: "This is not your shrine." Behind you, the thing in the shrine comes out, a fox with many tails, and looks at you, and at the sky, and walks out of the gate and down the mountain with its head down. The storm follows it a little way and goes out.

fail.log: You stand at the gate and the wind lifts you and puts you down in a pine tree. From there you watch the rain and the lightning go in, and a fox with many tails come out of the shrine into the open and bow to the sky. The lightning does not strike it. It walks away down the mountain. (-18 health)

choices.text: Go and fetch the old woman from the woodcutter's hut

effects.log: You run down to the hut and find the old woman sitting by the fire as calm as anything. "Is it time?" she asks. You carry her up the ridge on your back through the rain. At the shrine gate she gets down, and walks in, and something with many tails walks out past you, very quietly, without looking at either of you. The storm stops at once. The old woman lights the lamp in her shrine and goes to sleep.

choices.text: Stay down in the village with the frightened people

effects.log: You stay with the villagers, who are terrified, and keep them indoors and talking. The storm on the ridge goes on all night. In the morning the shrine is standing, the old woman is back in it sweeping, and the villagers, when they go up to pray, find that the goddess answers fewer prayers now, and they rather like her better for it.

events.text: On the mountain years after the storm, you meet a fox with many tails coming down the path from the old woman's shrine, carrying, very carefully in its mouth, a bundle of firewood.

choices.text: Step aside and let it pass

effects.log: You step aside. It passes, and puts the firewood down at the shrine's woodpile, and goes. The old woman, sweeping, tells you it comes every winter. "It took my shrine," she says. "It brings my wood. Foxes." She sounds, mostly, fond.

choices.text: Ask it why

effects.log: It puts the wood down. "They prayed to me," it says, around the bundle, with some difficulty. "It was very pleasant. It was not mine. Wood is mine." It picks the bundle up again and goes on up the path.

events.text: A grandmaster from the north, who has sworn to duel the Nine-Tailed Fox and has been looking for it for thirty years, has kicked open the wine-house gate and is pointing a great sword at you. "You," the grandmaster says. "Too calm. Too old for your face. Everyone in this province says the fox wears a master's face this year. Draw."

choices.text: Draw, and show them you are human the hard way

ok.log: You fight across the courtyard and over the roof and back, all evening, and at the end of it the grandmaster is sitting in the soup pot and you are standing over them with your sword at rest. "A fox," says the grandmaster, from the soup, "would have cheated." "Yes," you say. You help them out. Up on the roof ridge, briefly, something with a great many tails is watching, delighted.

fail.log: It is a long fight and you lose it, and lie in the courtyard with the grandmaster's sword at your throat. "You bleed red," the grandmaster says, disgusted, and leaves. As the gate bangs, a fox's sharp bark of a laugh comes from the roof, and the wine-house keeper, very carefully, does not look up. (-15 health)

choices.text: Offer the grandmaster a drink and a story instead

effects.log: "I am not the fox," you say, "but I have met one, and I will tell you about it if you put that away." The grandmaster, after a long moment, puts it away. You talk till dawn. In the morning the grandmaster says: "I have been looking for it so long I have forgotten why." When they leave, they leave the sword behind the counter.

events.text: The grandmaster from the north, much older, has written to you. "I have duelled the fox nine times now," the letter says, "and every time it was somebody else. A ferryman. A nun. A child. A very surprised magistrate. I begin to think the fox is arranging these meetings. They have all been very good fights. What should I do?"

choices.text: Write back: keep going, it is clearly enjoying itself

effects.log: You write it. The grandmaster writes back a year later: tenth fight, a wine-house keeper, a draw. At the end the keeper said, "Same time next year?" and the grandmaster, to their own great astonishment, said yes.

choices.text: Write back: stop looking, and it will find you

effects.log: You write it. The grandmaster stops. Two years later, at a crossroads, an old stranger sits down beside them on a bench, offers a cup of wine, and says: "I missed you." The grandmaster's last letter to you is all about it, and is very happy.

events.text: The old mountain spirit of the great peak has died, and for a year the mountain has had no one: springs run dry, the deer wander, the pines lean. Tonight, climbing to the summit to meditate, you find you are not alone. On the spirit's flat rock an old fox with a coat going black is sitting very still, and the whole mountain is turned toward it, like a field of grass in wind.
events.arc: A Fox Takes the Mountain's Seat

choices.text: Bow to it, as to the mountain

effects.log: You bow, low, as you would bow at a shrine. The fox looks at you, and dips its head. In that moment you feel the mountain settle around it like a robe around shoulders, and down in the valleys, all at once, the springs begin to run. You come down at dawn and tell nobody. The villages notice anyway.

choices.text: Ask it by what right

effects.log: "By what right?" you ask. The fox considers it. "I watched this mountain for a thousand years," it says. "I sent a young monk west to study, once, and I promised to keep them. The old spirit asked me. Nobody else would sit here and be bored for three thousand years." It pauses. "Do you want it?" You do not. It nods, as if relieved.

choices.text: Sit down on the next rock and keep it company

effects.log: You sit on the next rock. Neither of you says anything. The night goes by. At dawn the pines straighten and the springs run, and the fox, turning its black head, looks at you as if you had been a great help, which you suppose, in a way you do not understand, you were.

events.text: The mountain has a spirit again, and the villages below have begun to bring offerings to the summit: rice, chestnuts, wine. A rich family has brought a white fox fur, as the most precious thing they own. They want you, who first saw the spirit, to carry it up.
events.arc: A Fox Takes the Mountain's Seat

choices.text: Refuse, and tell them why

effects.log: You tell them, as gently as you can, what the mountain's spirit is. The family goes white, and then red, and takes the fur away and buries it under a pine with a proper rite. The next spring the family's spring runs sweet for the first time in a generation.

choices.text: Carry up rice instead, and say it is from them

effects.log: You leave the fur in a chest at the bottom of the mountain and carry up a sack of rice in the family's name. At the summit a black fox looks at the rice, and at you, with what you would swear is gratitude, and also with what you would swear is the knowledge of exactly what you left in the chest.

events.text: A young monk, newly back from eleven years of study across the western sea, has come up the great peak and is sitting under the pine below the summit, looking up at the flat rock with an expression you cannot read. "I dreamed of a black fox all the way home," the monk says. "I do not know why I am crying."
events.arc: A Fox Takes the Mountain's Seat

choices.text: Tell the monk who sits on the rock

effects.log: You tell the monk. The monk listens, and climbs the last stretch alone, and you watch from below as the young figure in grey kneels before the rock and the black fox comes down off it and touches its nose to the monk's forehead. They stay like that a long time. You go down the mountain and leave them to it.

choices.text: Say nothing; some things should be found

effects.log: You say nothing. The monk climbs on, and at the summit stops, and you see the black fox rise from the rock, and the monk run the last few steps like a child. You go down. Years later the monk's temple is built on that slope, and its name means the place of a promise.

events.text: There are very few people at your height of the art. One of them, a calm stranger who has been drinking tea with you on this terrace above the clouds every autumn for twenty years, puts down the cup tonight and says: "I am going to tell you a thing, and then you may decide whether to have tea with me again." Behind them, in the low sun, their shadow has nine tails.

choices.text: Ask which face is theirs

effects.log: "Which one is yours?" you ask. The stranger laughs, surprised. "None. All. This one, for you. I have had it twenty years, and I have grown fond of it, because you drink tea with it." You pour another cup. Neither of you says another word about it, and the next autumn you are both there.

choices.text: Say you knew in the third year

effects.log: "I knew in the third year," you say. "Your tea is too good." The stranger stares, then laughs until the tea slops. "Seventeen years," they say. "Seventeen years I have been worrying how to tell you." It is the best evening on that terrace in a few years.

choices.text: Get up and leave

effects.log: You get up and leave. It is not the tails. It is the twenty years. Next autumn you go up to the terrace anyway, and the stranger is there, with two cups, and the second one is still warm, as if they had poured it at exactly the moment you were deciding to come.

events.text: The stranger with nine tails who drinks tea with you every autumn has not come this year, and in their place on the terrace is a folded paper under a cup. It says: "Gone up the moon road to see if they will have me. If they do not, I shall be back for tea. If they do, pour mine anyway."

choices.text: Pour their cup anyway

effects.log: You pour two cups every autumn after. Most years the second one goes cold. One year, when you look away and back, the second cup is empty and there is a long pale hair on the cushion, the colour of moonlight.

choices.text: Climb as high as you can that night and look

effects.log: You climb to the highest rock on the peak at moonrise and look up. Far up, on a road of cloud, there is a small pale light walking toward the moon. It stops, once, and you could swear it looks back. Then it goes on.

events.text: Among the immortals there is a quiet one in grey, {npc}, who was a monk below in three lives and studied in the west in the first of them. Tonight {npc} has asked you to walk with {him} to a pine on a cloud-island. "I remember a black fox under a pine," {npc} says. "It sent me west. It kept me in my second life and my third. It died, I think, when I was old the third time. I have never thanked it."

choices.text: Help {npc} look for it

effects.log: You look all evening among the roots of the pine. At the foot of it, where the needles are thickest, you find a hollow the shape of a curled fox, warm, as if something had only just left it. {npc} kneels and puts {his} hand in the warmth and bows {his} head, and says thank you to the hollow, three times, once for each life.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the fox was to {him}

effects.log: "A neighbour who lost its temper with a noisy sorcerer and brought down a hillside," {npc} says, and smiles. "A teacher who sent me away when I wanted to stay. A promise. It took me three lives to understand that the promise was mine to keep as much as its."

choices.text: Suggest {npc} plant a pine of {his} own

effects.log: {npc} likes that. You plant one together on the cloud-island, a small pine in a hollow of moon-soil. In a century it is tall, and a black shadow is sometimes seen at its foot in the evenings, and {npc} sits there often, and is no longer sad.

events.text: {npc}, the immortal who was a monk three times, has had word: a black fox has been seen on the moon road, very old, walking slowly. {npc} wants to go and meet it, and is afraid of being too late again.

choices.text: Go with {npc}

effects.log: You go. On the moon road, where it leaves the clouds, an old black fox with a white muzzle is sitting, waiting, as if it knew. {npc} kneels in the moonlight. The fox touches its nose to {npc}'s forehead. You walk back alone, slowly, and {npc} comes down the road a long time after, and says nothing, and smiles for a century.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to go alone: some meetings are for two

effects.log: {npc} goes alone. You wait at the edge of the cloud. Long after midnight {npc} comes back and sits beside you and says: "I was not too late. It said I never could be. It said that was the whole point of a promise."

events.text: There is a temple far below, on a pine mountain, whose name means the place of a promise. From the edge of the clouds you can just see its roof. Every full moon, its monks leave a bowl of rice on a flat rock at the summit, and in the morning it is gone. Nobody below knows what for. You do.

choices.text: Send down a dream to the youngest monk, telling them

effects.log: You send a dream down: a black fox, a pine, a monk sent west. The youngest monk wakes weeping and runs to the abbot, who listens and says only: "Yes. Keep leaving the rice." They do. You are glad someone below knows.

choices.text: Leave it a mystery; mysteries keep rice bowls full

effects.log: You leave it. Some things are better as a custom than as a story. A thousand years on, the monks are still leaving rice, and still do not know why, and the rice is still gone in the morning, and on the summit rock, very faint, is a smell of earth and moon.

events.text: You are called to testify at a hearing of the Four Guardians: the Azure Dragon of the east, the White Tiger of the west, the Vermilion Bird of the south, the Black Tortoise of the north, and the Yellow Dragon at the centre. The question is whether a fox may sit at their table. Of all the humans who ever lived, the fox asked for you as a witness, because, it says, you once saw it at its worst and its best. You are not sure which it means.

choices.text: Testify to the best of it

effects.log: You tell the Guardians the kindest thing you ever saw it do. The Dragon's voice asks about a dyke and an egg; the Tiger's, about a wine-house; you answer what you know. At the end the fox, on its little cushion, looks at you as if you had carried something heavy a long way for it.

choices.text: Testify to everything, the worst first

effects.log: You tell it all, worst first: the pale ones, the breath, the faces. Then the rest. The court is silent a long time. "It asked for you," the Tortoise says at last, slowly, "knowing you would do this." "Yes," says the fox. "Heaven should not be lied to by its witnesses." Something in the four great seats shifts, like weather changing.

choices.text: Refuse to testify about a friend

effects.log: "I will not testify," you say. "It is a friend." The court murmurs. The fox, on its cushion, laughs out loud, a short sharp bark that echoes through heaven. "There," it says to the four seats. "That is all I wanted you to see. Somebody calls me friend."

events.text: After the hearing a messenger brings you a single long pale hair, the colour of moonlight, wrapped in a cloud-silk cloth. No word with it. The Guardians' verdict, you are told, is not published. But tonight, for the first time anyone can remember, there are five lamps lit at the Guardians' table instead of four.

choices.text: Climb to where you can see the table and count again

effects.log: You climb. Five lamps, and at the fifth, small, on a round cushion, a shape of moonlight with its tail around its feet. It turns its head toward you across all that distance. You raise your hand. It dips its head. That is all, and it is plenty.

choices.text: Keep the hair and say nothing to anyone

effects.log: You keep the hair in your sleeve. On the night of every full moon after, it glows, faintly, the way a lamp glows behind a paper door when someone you know is home.

events.text: An immortal envoy in jade-green robes has been sent to audit the breath-ledger of every fox in the land below, and has asked you to be the second signature. The ledger is enormous: every breath borrowed, every breath given back. Some columns balance. Some do not.

choices.text: Read every column, slowly

effects.log: You read every column for a year. You learn that a fox of the hill road gave back every breath it ever took, and one more; that a wine-house fox never took any; that one fox in the south took a hundred and the hundredth woke. You sign at the end. The envoy looks at your signature and says, "Most people sign at the beginning."

choices.text: Ask why only foxes are audited

effects.log: "Why only foxes?" you ask. "Humans borrow breath from each other all their lives." The envoy is silent. Then, slowly, the envoy takes out a second, much larger ledger, unbound, and looks at it a long time, and puts it away again. "That one is not mine to keep," the envoy says. You both sign the fox ledger, and neither of you is entirely comfortable.

events.text: The envoy of the breath-ledger has found an error. One fox's column shows a debt of one breath that was never repaid: a student on a hill road, long ago, who swallowed the bead. The fox's case at the Guardians' table hangs on it. And the student, you realise as you read the name, was in one of your own past lives.

choices.text: Write in the margin: the debt was forgiven

effects.log: You write it in your own hand: forgiven, freely, by the one it was owed to. The envoy reads it, and nods, and closes the ledger, which now balances. Somewhere below, on a hill road at dusk, foxes sit up on every grave mound and look at the sky.

choices.text: Write: it was not a debt; I was given the earth

effects.log: You write: not a debt. A gift, taken clumsily, and I have had the use of it in every life since. The envoy reads it twice, and laughs, and moves the line from the column of debts to the column of gifts, where there are not very many lines at all.

events.text: At the foot of the moon road, where it leaves the last cloud, a fox the colour of moonlight is sitting, waiting. "I was told a sovereign could walk it with me," it says, "so that it is not only foxes who know the way. It is a long road. I would like the company. I would like a human to see what is at the top."

choices.text: Walk the moon road beside it

effects.log: You walk beside it, step for step, at arm's length, all night. It tells you about grave mounds and hill roads and wine-houses, and you tell it about your lives. At the top there is nothing but light, and the fox walks into it, and turns once, and you see a face in the light that might be anybody's. Then you are walking down alone, and it is dawn, and you know the way.

choices.text: Walk a little way, and come back

effects.log: You walk until the clouds are far below and the moon is too bright to look at, and then you stop. "This is as far as I go," you say. The fox nods. "That is further than anyone has," it says. It goes on alone. You watch it until it is a small pale light, and then a star.

choices.text: Ask it why it wants a human to see

effects.log: "Because humans tell the stories," it says. "For two thousand years you have told stories about the fox on the hill road. I would like one of you to tell the end." You walk with it, after that, as far as you can, and you tell the end, afterwards, to everyone who will listen.

events.text: Since you walked the moon road, the foxes of the world below have been sitting on the grave mounds on full moon nights and looking up, and the people below have noticed, and are frightened, and are praying to heaven to stop it. The petition has reached your desk.

choices.text: Answer the petition with the true story

effects.log: You write the answer as a story, plainly: a fox that went up the road, and the foxes below looking at where it went. It is read out in a thousand villages. The next full moon, people sit on the grave mounds too, at a respectful distance from the foxes, and look up.

choices.text: Let the fear pass on its own

effects.log: You set the petition aside. In a generation the fear is a custom, and in two it is a festival, with rice cakes left on the grave mounds on the full moon, and children told that the foxes are watching the road to heaven. That is close enough to true.

events.text: A sovereign of heaven, old and stern, has proposed to close the moon road to foxes for ever. "They take breath," the sovereign says. "They wear faces. One climbed. Now all of them look up. Heaven is not a reward for pretending." The council will vote. Your seal is one of nine.
events.arc: The Closing of the Moon Road

choices.text: Vote to keep the road open

effects.log: "Every one of us pretended to be something better than we were," you say, "and some of us became it. That is all the road is." Five seals to four. The road stays open. The stern sovereign, leaving, says to you very quietly: "I hope you are right. I would like to be."

choices.text: Vote to close it, but only to foxes who will not repay

ok.log: You rewrite the motion on the council floor: the road open to any fox whose ledger balances, closed to any whose does not. It passes nine to none. The stern sovereign looks at you with something like respect. "That is fairer than heaven is to most immortals," the sovereign says.

fail.log: You try to rewrite the motion and it tangles in its own clauses, and the council, bored, votes on the original: four to five, the road stays open, mostly by accident. You are not proud of the speech. You are glad of the result.

choices.text: Vote to close it

effects.log: You vote to close it. Four to five: it stays open anyway. That night a long pale hair is on your desk, laid very neatly across your seal, and you cannot tell whether it is a reproach or a thank you for honesty. Probably both.

events.text: The stern sovereign who wanted the moon road closed has come to you, in private, without a seal. "I was a student once," the sovereign says, "on a hill road, a very long time ago. A stranger walked beside me every evening. I never knew what I should have done. I closed the road because I could not close that."
events.arc: The Closing of the Moon Road

choices.text: Tell the sovereign the old story, all of it

effects.log: You tell it: sky, earth, people; the swallowing and the giving back; the hundredth one who always wakes. The sovereign listens like a child. "There was no right answer," the sovereign says at last. "There were only answers." "Yes," you say. The sovereign goes away much lighter.

choices.text: Walk with the sovereign to the foot of the moon road

effects.log: You walk to the foot of the road together. A fox of moonlight is sitting there. The sovereign stops. The fox looks up and says, very gently, the sovereign's name from a life two thousand years ago. You leave them to talk. When you look back they are walking up the road, side by side, at arm's length.

events.text: Rain from a clear sky: the sun shining full on the paddies and the rain coming down through it, warm and silver. The old people in the village look up and say: fox rain. A tiger is getting married today. On the far ridge, through the bright mist, you think you see a line of striped shadows walking in procession.

choices.text: Stand out in it and laugh

effects.log: You stand in the field with your face turned up and laugh, and the rain is warm and smells of grass. The old people say it is good luck for the tiger's marriage, rain on a wedding day. You decide it is good luck for you too. It is, more or less, all year.

choices.text: Watch the ridge

effects.log: You watch the ridge. The striped shadows go along it slowly, a long procession, and at the edge of the paddy, between you and them, a small red-brown fox is sitting in the sunny rain watching them too. It notices you. You both go back to watching. It feels like a holiday.

choices.text: Ask the old people why it is called fox rain

effects.log: Everyone has a different answer. A fox crying for someone it loves, and heaven crying with it. A fox tricking the tiger at its wedding. A fox who was the tiger's bride. The oldest grandmother says: "Because foxes are the only ones who notice that rain and sun can happen at once." You like hers best.

events.text: Fox rain again, years later, sun and rain together over a different valley. This time you are on the road, alone, and a stranger in a plain jacket is standing under the same pine you shelter under, smiling at the rain as if it were an old friend's joke.

choices.text: Say: a tiger is marrying today

effects.log: "A tiger is marrying today," you say. The stranger laughs. "So they say. I was invited. I sent my regrets. Weddings make me cry." When the rain stops and you step out from the pine, the stranger is not there, and on the dry earth under the pine, where they stood, there are fox prints.

choices.text: Share your rice ball

effects.log: You break your rice ball in two and hold out half. The stranger takes it, astonished, and eats it in tiny bites. "Nobody shares in fox rain," they say. "Everybody hurries." The rain stops. You walk on together as far as the crossroads, and talk about nothing, and it is a very good hour.

events.text: Crossing the marsh causeway at night, you see lights out over the reeds: pale, drifting, low, three of them, then five. The ferryman told you this morning: foxfire. Follow it, and you will walk all night and come out where you started, if you are lucky. If you are a cruel landlord, the ferryman added, you come out in the paddy.

choices.text: Keep to the causeway and do not look

effects.log: You keep your eyes on the causeway stones and walk. The lights drift alongside for a while, curious, and then, bored, drift off. You reach the far bank at midnight and laugh at yourself. Behind you, out on the marsh, something laughs too.

choices.text: Follow one, and see

ok.log: You follow. The light leads you along a path you could never have found, dry-footed, through the reeds, and out on the far bank an hour sooner than the causeway would have. It goes out at the bank like a blown lamp. You feel you have been helped by someone who wanted to show off.

fail.log: You follow, and walk all night, and come out at dawn exactly where you started, wet to the knees, with a frog in your sleeve. The ferryman, seeing you, does not even ask. (-4 health)

choices.text: Bow to the lights and ask for a safe crossing

effects.log: You bow to the marsh and ask, politely, for a safe crossing. The lights gather, all five, and hang over the causeway ahead of you all the way across, like lanterns at a wedding. On the far bank they go out one by one. You bow again. It seems only right.

events.text: The new landlord of the marsh villages is a cruel one: double rents, the granary locked in a hungry spring. Tonight he is riding home late across the marsh causeway with his bailiffs, and you, by chance, are on the far bank. Out over the reeds, the lights are coming up.

choices.text: Shout to warn him off the causeway

effects.log: You shout. He does not listen to commoners. The lights lead him off the causeway, and he spends the night up to his waist in his own paddy, with the bailiffs, shouting. In the morning he opens the granary, for reasons he does not explain. The marsh villages do not explain anything either.

choices.text: Say nothing, and watch

effects.log: You say nothing. The lights lead him round the marsh until dawn, gently, without harm, and deposit him at his own gate soaked and terrified. The rents go down by half that summer. On the marsh, the next night, the lights come out in a little dance, and you would swear one of them bows to you.

events.text: The yellow dog that lives in your yard, which has never barked at anything but the moon, will not stop barking at the guest room. A traveller is staying the night: a polite, quiet traveller who paid in advance and asked for no lamp. The dog's hackles are up. It is staring at the paper door, where the traveller's shadow sits very still.

choices.text: Take the dog inside and shut it in the kitchen

effects.log: You shut the dog in the kitchen. In the morning the traveller is gone, the room is swept, the bedding is folded with absolute precision, and on the pillow there is a small bundle of good dried persimmons and a single red-brown hair. The dog sniffs the pillow and, for some reason, wags.

choices.text: Let the dog bark, and light a lamp in the yard

effects.log: You light a lamp in the yard. In the lamplight the shadow on the paper door has a tail, just one, which twitches. Then the lamp in the yard goes out by itself, and in the dark the traveller says quietly through the door: "I will be gone at first light. Tell your dog it is a very good dog." And is.

choices.text: Knock and tell the traveller your dog is uneasy

effects.log: "My dog is uneasy," you say through the door. A silence. Then: "Dogs are wise," says the traveller. "I apologise to your dog." The barking stops, abruptly, as if somebody had explained something. In the morning the traveller and the dog are sitting together on the step, looking at each other with great mutual suspicion and some respect.

events.text: The old yellow dog that lives in your yard is dying, grey-muzzled, by the stove. At dusk, there is a scratch at the gate. When you open it, a red-brown fox is sitting there, quite still, and looks past you at the stove.

choices.text: Stand aside and let it in

effects.log: You stand aside. The fox walks in, across the yard, into the kitchen, and lies down a little way from the old dog, and the old dog lifts its head and looks at it, and puts its head down again, and its tail moves twice on the floor. In the morning the dog is gone, peacefully, and so is the fox, and you never know what was said.

choices.text: Shut the gate: the dog barked at foxes all its life

effects.log: You shut the gate. The fox stays outside it all night. In the morning the old dog is gone, and the fox has gone, and outside the gate, set neatly on the step, is a bone, the kind a dog likes. You bury it with the dog.

events.text: A merchant who has just lost a long argument with you over the price of rope throws up their hands and calls you what people call anyone too clever by half: a hundred-year fox. The whole market laughs. Then, from under the merchant's stall, very quietly, something that is not a dog sneezes.

choices.text: Say: a hundred years is young

effects.log: "A hundred years is young," you say. "Ask me again at a thousand." The market roars. Under the stall, something sneezes twice, in what sounds very much like approval. You get your rope at your price.

choices.text: Look under the stall

effects.log: You look under the stall. Nothing but a basket of turnips and, behind it, a pair of amber eyes, which close, slowly, in what in a cat would be a greeting. You straighten up and pay the merchant's price after all. It seems the least you can do.

events.text: You are old now, and the young people of the district have begun to call you a thousand-year fox behind your back, with respect. One of them is bold enough to say it to your face, and to ask whether you mind.

choices.text: Say it is the best compliment you have had

effects.log: "The best," you say. "Foxes know how to stay alive among people who would rather they did not. So do the old." The young one goes away thinking about that. That night, on your roof, something walks very lightly from one end to the other and back, and stops, and sits, keeping you company.

choices.text: Tell them about a real fox you once knew

effects.log: You tell them about the fox you once knew. They listen, round-eyed, and then, being young, do not believe a word. But one of them goes up to the grave mounds at dusk with a rice cake, to see, and comes back very quiet, and never calls anybody a fox as an insult again.

events.text: The old widow at the end of the lane, who used to leave rice cakes by the grave mounds for "the stray", is in her last winter. She has no one: her son died at sea, and his wife went away years ago. And now, the neighbours say, the son's wife has come back, in a plain white jacket, and is nursing her day and night. Nobody saw her arrive. She does not look a day older than when she left.

choices.text: Bring firewood, and say nothing

effects.log: You bring firewood every week. The daughter-in-law thanks you with a bow and eyes that catch the fire. The old widow, warm and fed and talking about her son, dies in the spring, smiling, holding a hand she believes is her daughter-in-law's. The daughter-in-law cuts the grass on the new mound, and is gone.

choices.text: Ask the old widow whether she knows

effects.log: You ask, gently, when the daughter-in-law is out at the well. The old widow laughs, a cracked happy laugh. "Of course I know," she says. "My son's wife never once made porridge this well. I fed it rice cakes for years. It is feeding me back. Leave us be."

events.text: Chuseok, and you go up to the old widow's mound with a sickle, since she has no one. The grass is already cut, very neatly. On the flat stone is a rice cake, the kind she used to make, and it is still warm.

choices.text: Leave one of your own beside it

effects.log: You set your own rice cake beside it and bow to the mound and to the long grass behind it. When you look back from the path, both rice cakes are still there, side by side, and a red-brown fox is sitting by the mound, not eating either, only keeping them company.

choices.text: Sit by the mound a while

effects.log: You sit a while in the autumn sun. After a time you notice that someone is sitting at the other end of the mound, in a white jacket, not looking at you, also keeping the widow company. Neither of you speaks. It is very peaceful.

events.text: In the wine-house below the pass a huge quiet stranger is drinking alone in the corner, and paid for the wine with a whole deer, laid by the door wrapped in straw. The keeper served the stranger without a flicker. You are sitting between them, and you have the most peculiar feeling that each of them knows exactly what the other is, and that neither of them is human. A squad of tiger-catching soldiers is clattering into the yard.
events.arc: The Guest Who Is Not a Guest

choices.text: Start a loud argument with the soldiers about the road tax

effects.log: You pick a quarrel with the sergeant about the road tax, loudly, at length, with figures. By the time the soldiers have finished shouting at you, the corner table is empty, and the deer is gone, and the keeper is wiping a perfectly clean counter. The sergeant buys you a bowl of noodles in the end, for the entertainment.

choices.text: Say nothing and finish your soup

effects.log: You finish your soup. The soldiers ask the keeper if anyone strange has come by. "Nobody stranger than you," the keeper says sweetly, and they laugh, and drink, and go. The huge stranger in the corner, all this while, has simply not been noticed by anybody, which you begin to think is the strangest thing of all.

choices.text: Tell the sergeant there is a tiger in the corner

effects.log: You point. The sergeant looks at the corner: a large, mild, slightly sleepy traveller, who raises a cup to him. The sergeant looks at you. "Too much wine," he says, and the soldiers laugh at you all night. In the morning, on your pillow, there are a few long white and black hairs and one red-brown one. You think you were warned by two people at once.

events.text: Years later you meet the huge quiet stranger from the wine-house again, on a mountain pass in the first snow. "The keeper at the crossroads," the stranger says, in a voice like a rockfall, "asks after you. We sit up together sometimes. Neither of us has much company that understands."
events.arc: The Guest Who Is Not a Guest

choices.text: Send the keeper your regards

effects.log: "Tell the keeper I still think about the soup," you say. The stranger nods, gravely, and goes on up the pass. You notice, when you look back, that the snow behind you is printed not with boots but with great round pads, and then, a little way on, with small neat fox prints going the other way.

choices.text: Ask what two such guests talk about

effects.log: The stranger thinks. "People," the stranger says at last. "Whether they are worth it. The keeper always says yes. I mostly say yes. You are one of the reasons." Then the stranger is a shape in the snow, and then not.

events.text: At the village harvest feast there is a guest everybody seems to know and nobody can name: a cheerful, very greedy guest with a face that does not quite fit, as if it had been borrowed from someone a size smaller. The guest has eaten nine bowls of buckwheat jelly and challenged the whole village to wrestling. Leaning against the wall behind, there is a knobbly wooden club that nobody brought.
events.arc: The Dokkaebi Who Wanted a Face

choices.text: Wrestle the guest

ok.log: You wrestle, and throw the guest, and the borrowed face slips sideways for a moment and underneath is something with a horn and a great grin. The guest roars with laughter and gives you a lump of silver that turns into a perfectly good turnip by morning. A dokkaebi, you understand, and a borrowed face, and you wonder whose.

fail.log: The guest throws you over the drum. Everybody cheers. The guest helps you up with a hand that is much too large and calls you a fine fellow and eats your buckwheat jelly. (-5 health)

choices.text: Ask the guest where the face came from

effects.log: "Borrowed it," says the guest cheerfully, "from a fox on the hill. For one night. I promised to bring it back by cockcrow." The guest prods the face. "I may have dented it a bit." You look at the forehead. There is a small, club-shaped dent. The guest seems unconcerned.

events.text: Some time after the harvest feast, a quiet person in a plain jacket stops you on the road. They have a small dent in their forehead, the exact shape of a club. "Did you see a dokkaebi at the feast in my face?" they ask, with terrible patience. "I lent it for one night. I would like to know how much of it I have to apologise for."
events.arc: The Dokkaebi Who Wanted a Face

choices.text: Tell them everything, buckwheat jelly and all

effects.log: You tell them all of it, the nine bowls, the wrestling, the drum. They listen with their eyes closed. "Nine bowls," they say at last. "In my face." Then, to your surprise, they start to laugh, and cannot stop, and have to sit down on a rock by the road.

choices.text: Say it behaved itself very well

effects.log: "It behaved itself beautifully," you lie. They look at you with great gratitude, and you know they know, and they know you know. You part as friends. The dent, they mention, will take about ten years to grow out.

events.text: You are a captain of the palace guard in a kingdom that everyone knows is failing: famine in the south, war on the border, a king who listens only to flatterers. This spring, foxes have been seen in the palace gardens. This morning, in plain daylight, a white fox walked past your guards into the hall of the chief minister and sat down on the chief minister's desk, among the papers, and is still sitting there.
events.arc: The Fox on the Minister's Desk

choices.text: Leave it there, and send for the chief minister to see it

effects.log: The chief minister comes and stands in the doorway and looks at the fox for a long time, and the fox looks back. Then the minister goes, without a word, to the king, and for the first time in ten years says something true to the king. It does not save the kingdom. It is written down, though, in the histories: the spring the fox sat on the desk, and the one minister who spoke.

choices.text: Drive it out with your guards

roll.foeName: The white fox on the desk

ok.log: You drive it out with spears, and it goes, unhurried, through the gardens and over the wall. The court says the omen is broken. The court is wrong. But you did your duty, and the histories, when they are written, do not mention you at all, which you come to think is a mercy.

fail.log: Your spears find only papers. The fox is simply on the desk, and then not, and then on the roof ridge, and then nowhere. The whole palace saw. The histories write it down. (-5 health)

choices.text: Write it down yourself, plainly, for the record

effects.log: You write it plainly in the guard's day-book: a white fox, the chief minister's desk, the hour of the snake, nobody harmed. Two hundred years later, a scholar reading the histories of the fallen kingdom will find your plain line in a guard's day-book and use it, and be grateful for its plainness.

events.text: The kingdom fell, as everyone knew it would. You are old, serving the new one, and a young historian of the new court has come to ask you about the white fox on the desk. "Was it an omen?" the historian asks. "Or was it only a fox?"
events.arc: The Fox on the Minister's Desk

choices.text: Say: it was a fox, and the omen was us

effects.log: "It was a fox," you say. "The omen was a palace where a fox could walk in at noon and sit on the chief minister's desk and nobody had stopped it for a month." The historian writes that down. It is in the histories still, next to the fox.

choices.text: Say: I think it came to warn us

effects.log: "I think it came to warn us," you say. "It sat there in plain sight, so that we would have to look." The historian writes that down too, and later, privately, asks if you think the foxes are watching the new court. You say yes. The historian goes away thoughtful.

events.text: On full moon nights in this province, people say, the foxes sit on the grave mounds and look up. Tonight you see it for yourself: a hillside of mounds, and on almost every one a fox, sitting very upright, looking at the moon. There is a faint pale line across the sky from the hill to the moon, like a road of cloud. You feel, unaccountably, that you ought to know where it goes.

choices.text: Sit down on the path and look up with them

effects.log: You sit on the path and look up. Nobody moves. After a long while, very far along the pale road, you see a small light walking, and every fox on the hillside makes a soft sound together, like a breath let out. You go home before dawn with the strangest feeling that someone you once were is very proud of something.

choices.text: Bow to the moon, as the foxes do

effects.log: You bow, as low as the foxes. The nearest one turns its head and looks at you, surprised, and then, quite deliberately, bows back. The whole of the next month, every dog in the district wags at you.

events.text: A child from the next house asks why the foxes look at the moon. Everyone else has given them a different story. They want yours.

choices.text: Tell them: one of them went up, and they are watching the road

effects.log: "One of them went up," you say. "It took a thousand years, and it gave back everything it took. They are watching the road, to remember the way." The child thinks about this very seriously. That night, you find them sitting on your step looking up at the moon with great concentration, and you sit down beside them.

choices.text: Take them out on the next full moon to see

effects.log: You take them to the hill on the full moon. The foxes are there, on every mound. The child holds your hand very hard and says nothing at all, and on the way home asks only, "Can people go up it too?" You find you are almost sure the answer is yes.

events.text: The mountain is called Long-Arm Mountain, for a reason the villages argue about, and under the great pine below its summit there is a small shrine with a painting of a black fox with a white muzzle. The monks of the temple below leave rice there every full moon. When you stand before the painting, your eyes sting, and you do not know why.

choices.text: Leave rice with the monks' rice

effects.log: You leave a bowl beside the monks'. An old monk, sweeping, watches you do it, and says, "The temple was founded on a promise. A fox kept a monk through three lives. We are still keeping our half." On the way down the mountain, every pine you pass seems to lean, very slightly, toward you.

choices.text: Ask the old monk about the painting

effects.log: "Three thousand years old when it died," the old monk says, "under this pine. The monk it kept found it, the third time round, and named the mountain for the promise." The monk looks at you curiously. "You have the look of someone who has heard this before."

events.text: Lost on Long-Arm Mountain in a sudden autumn fog, with night coming and the cliffs close, you hear a fox bark, once, ahead of you on the path.

choices.text: Follow it

effects.log: You follow the bark, and it comes again, and again, always a little ahead, until the fog thins and you are standing at the temple gate. No fox. Only, on the gate step, a few black hairs, white at the tip. You add a second bowl of rice at the shrine the next morning.

choices.text: Stay still, as the old monks advise

effects.log: You stay still, as the monks say to in fog. The fox's bark comes nearer, and then a shape is sitting beside you on the path, dark, with a white muzzle, warm against your side all night, keeping the cold off. At dawn the fog lifts, and the shape is gone, and you walk down safe.

events.text: Your family has an old joke: everyone in it has cold feet, winter and summer, and dogs never quite trust any of you, and you have the best luck in the district. The family tree goes back five generations to an ancestor who came from nowhere, with no family, and lived to ninety, and never once lied about it, and never once explained it.

choices.text: Ask your oldest relative about the ancestor

effects.log: Your oldest relative laughs. "They said: I was something else once, and then I was this, and this is better. That is all they ever said." A pause. "They also said that if a fox ever sits on the step, give it a rice cake. It is family."

choices.text: Put on thicker socks and be grateful for the luck

effects.log: You put on the thick quilted socks the family always wears, and sit on the warm floor, and are grateful. That evening there is a red-brown fox sitting at the bottom of the yard, looking at the house the way people look at a house they used to live in. The dog does not bark.

events.text: At the market a pedlar is selling a spirit fox, a little red-brown thing with a white chest, in a bamboo cage. It looks at you through the bars as if it has been waiting for you, specifically, for about a hundred years.

choices.text: Buy it and open the cage at the edge of town (5 taels)

effects.log: You pay five taels and carry it to the edge of town and open the cage. It does not run. It walks beside you all the way home, and curls up on your step, and stays. The dogs of your family, for the first time in five generations, decide to trust somebody.

choices.text: Talk to it through the bars

effects.log: You crouch and talk to it, nonsense, the way you would to a baby. It listens with its head on one side. Then the pedlar turns his back for a moment, and the cage is empty, and the door is still shut. That night it is on your step.

events.text: You have married into, or been taken into, or simply found work with, a family of geomancers that has never once chosen a bad site in three hundred years. In the place of honour hangs an old wooden compass, and beneath it, in a lacquer box, a small dim pearl. Family rule: never put it in your mouth. Family joke: and never look at the sky.

choices.text: Ask why never the sky

effects.log: "Because the founder looked at the earth," the eldest says, "by falling down. A fox gave the bead on purpose, and said look at the sky, and the founder fell and saw the earth. For years after, the founder heard a voice in one ear telling them where the water was." The eldest smiles. "We think the voice wanted us to keep looking down. It is where people live."

choices.text: Hold the box, just for a moment

effects.log: You hold the lacquer box. It is warm. Through the wood, faintly, you feel the hill under the house, cold and warm in veins, and for a moment a voice in your ear, very old and very fond, says: three paces to the left. You put it down at once. The family, watching, nods as if you had passed something.

events.text: A drought, and the village well is dry, and the geomancers' family is asked where to dig. They look at you, because last night, in a dream, you heard a voice say exactly where.

choices.text: Say where the voice said

effects.log: You say it: three paces from the old pine, a man's height down. They dig. Water, cold and fast. The family looks at you a long time, and that evening the eldest moves your sleeping mat to the room under the compass.

choices.text: Say you dreamed it, and let them decide

effects.log: You tell them it was only a dream. The eldest goes very still and asks what the voice sounded like. You try to describe it: old, amused, a little rough, like a fox's bark made into a word. The eldest goes and digs by the pine, alone, and finds water.

events.text: Your family is descended, they say, from the general the villages called fox-born, who could catch tigers and was found as a baby at a grave mound. In the family shrine, below the general's portrait, there is a small carving of a fox. And there is a family rule nobody outside understands: never hunt, never cut wood, on the hill above the old house.

choices.text: Keep the rule, and go up the hill at Chuseok

effects.log: You go up at Chuseok with a sickle and rice cakes. Near the top there is a small old mound nobody in the family will name. You cut its grass with the others. When you stand up, there is a fox sitting at the edge of the pines, young and quick, watching you exactly the way the general in the portrait watches the room.

choices.text: Ask the oldest relative what the carving is for

effects.log: "For the one who raised the general," the oldest says. "A herb-seller who was never seen by lamplight. The general put a fox on the shrine and never said why. We keep it dusted." A pause. "Your hands are very quick, you know. You get that from somebody."

events.text: A tiger has come down into the valley in a hard winter, and the villagers have run to your family, because the general's descendants, everybody knows, can catch tigers. You are not at all sure you can.

choices.text: Go out to meet it

ok.log: You go out, and are quicker than you have any right to be, quick as the stories, and the tiger, startled, cuffed, turns tail and goes back up the mountain. The village cheers. On the way home, from the hill above the old house, you hear a fox bark, once, very pleased.

fail.log: You go out, and the tiger knocks you flat, and stands over you, and then, for no reason anybody can see, looks up at the hill above the old house, and goes away up the mountain. You lie in the snow and laugh. Some help is family. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell the truth: the stories are old, and you are no general

effects.log: You tell them. They are disappointed. So you all bang pots together, the whole village, all night, and the tiger, deafened, goes home. In the morning there are small fox prints all round your house, as if somebody had been pacing.

events.text: There is a wine-house at a crossroads that has been there, they say, five hundred years, under one keeper after another. Every traveller who stops there gets home: it is a proverb on four roads. The soup has radish greens in it. The kitchen wall is black with five centuries of charcoal tally-marks for makgeolli on credit. When you walk in, the keeper looks up and, for one moment, looks as if they have seen a ghost, or an old friend.

choices.text: Order soup, and stay the night

effects.log: The soup is the best you have ever eaten, and also, impossibly, familiar, as if you had once made it yourself. In the morning the keeper will not take your money. "Paid," says the keeper, and points to the wall, to a very old tally-mark, crossed out, beside a name you do not know and somehow do.

choices.text: Ask about the old marks on the kitchen wall

effects.log: The keeper shows you: five hundred years of debts, almost all crossed out. "The first keeper never let anyone go home owing," says the keeper. "In the end, the first keeper went, and the wine-house stayed, and so do we." You find, among the oldest marks, one shaped like a small fox's paw.

events.text: A blizzard on the pass, and you are lost in it, and certain you will die, when you see, below, a light: paper lanterns at a crossroads where you are sure there was nothing on the way up.

choices.text: Go down to the light

effects.log: You stumble in at the door and a bowl of hot soup is put into your hands before you have said a word. The keeper sits with you till dawn. In the morning, on the pass in the sun, you look back, and there is the wine-house, and you walk home, as everybody who stops there does.

choices.text: Shout for help instead
