effects.log: You shout. A small red-brown shape comes up the snow from the lanterns, and stops a pace off, and turns, and waits. You follow it down. At the door it is gone, and the keeper is there, ladle in hand, as if you had been expected for hours.

events.text: Your family has an old house, and in it an old story: an ancestor married someone who asked only one thing, that for a hundred days they would not be looked at while they slept. On the ninety-ninth night the ancestor looked. In the morning the one they loved was gone, and the house was full of everything they had owned, left neatly, and a set of fox tracks went up the mountain in the frost. It is the most told story in the district.

choices.text: Ask whether the ancestor ever forgave themself

effects.log: "Never," says the oldest of the family. "And never stopped leaving the door open at night, for years, in case." A pause. "There was no revenge. That is the part people forget. It could have taken everything. It left everything instead."

choices.text: Go up the mountain path and look

effects.log: You go up the path. Near the top there is a flat rock with a view of the old house. The moss on it is worn smooth in one place, the size of a sitting fox, as if something had sat there and watched the house for a very long time.

events.text: Someone you love has asked you for something that seems small and strange: not to ask them about one particular thing, ever, for a hundred days. You find the old family story going round and round in your head.

choices.text: Keep the promise, all hundred days

effects.log: You keep it, a hundred days, never asking, never looking. On the hundred-and-first morning they tell you, of their own accord, and it turns out to be something small and sad and human, a debt, an old shame, and you are the first person they ever told. You go up the mountain path that evening and leave a rice cake on the flat rock.

choices.text: Tell them the old family story first

effects.log: You tell them the story of the ninety-ninth night. They listen, and laugh a little, and say, "Then you know how much it matters." You keep the promise. On the hundred-and-first morning the door of your house is open, and there is frost on the step, and no tracks at all, which you decide is a good sign.

events.text: Reading the old histories of a fallen kingdom, you come to the spring before the end: "a white fox entered the palace and sat upon the chief minister's desk." Some scholar long ago has painted, in the margin, a tiny white fox. Your hands are cold. You have the absurd feeling that you remember the smell of the minister's ink.

choices.text: Read on, and see what the court did

effects.log: The court did nothing, of course. One minister spoke; one guard wrote it down plainly. The kingdom fell. You read the plain line in the guard's day-book three times. It is the only line in the whole history that does not lie, and you close the book feeling, strangely, that you were thanked.

choices.text: Ask the archivist about the painted fox

effects.log: "Every copy has it," the archivist says. "Every copyist adds one. Nobody remembers who started it." The archivist looks at you. "Some of us think the fox was not the sign of the end. Some of us think it was the only one in the palace who came to look."

events.text: At court, a minister is about to lie to the king about a famine in the south. Every official in the hall knows it. You are a junior, at the back. A white cat walks into the hall, ignored by everyone, and sits down on the minister's desk.

choices.text: Speak up about the famine

ok.log: You speak. The hall goes silent, and the king looks at the cat on the desk, and at you, and asks for the southern reports. The famine relief goes out in a week. The cat, when you look again, is not there, and was, someone insists later, not a cat at all.

fail.log: You speak and are shouted down. But the king, leaving, glances at the minister's desk, where a white animal is sitting looking at him, and stops, and asks quietly for the southern reports. The relief goes out late. It goes out.

choices.text: Stay silent, and watch the cat

effects.log: You stay silent. The minister lies. The cat on the desk watches the minister the whole time, without blinking. That night you cannot sleep, and in the morning you write the southern reports out fair and leave them on the king's secretary's desk, and you never know if that is why.

events.text: Cutting the grass on an old grave mound at Chuseok, you find an earth dug under it, and in the earth, alone, one small red-brown kit, eyes not yet open, mewing. Its mother is nowhere. When your shadow falls across the entrance, it stops mewing and turns its blind face toward you, exactly as if it knew who you were.

choices.text: Leave rice and water, and come back every day

effects.log: You come back every day for a month with rice gruel and water. The kit's eyes open on the ninth day, and the first thing they see is you, and it looks at you not like a kit at all, but like something very old, tired, and grateful. On the last day it is gone, and there are small prints going up the hill, and a peeled chestnut at the entrance.

choices.text: Leave it: its mother will come

effects.log: You leave it. At dusk you come back to look, and there is a vixen at the entrance with two tails, which she hides at once, and she looks at you, and you go away. You are not sure, afterwards, whether she was its mother or someone keeping an old promise.

events.text: A young fox with one tail has taken to sitting on the wall of your yard in the evenings, watching you go about your work. It is not afraid. It looks at you, sometimes, as if it is about to say something, and then decides not to.

choices.text: Talk to it about your day

effects.log: You talk to it about your day while you work: the price of rice, a quarrel with a neighbour. It listens with its ears forward. Years later, when it has two tails, it is still there most evenings, and once, very quietly, it says your name.

choices.text: Ask it whether it remembers

effects.log: "Do you remember?" you ask it. The young fox looks at you a long time. Then it nods, once, very clearly, the way a person nods, and jumps down off the wall and goes. In the morning there is a chestnut on the step. You understand that it is starting again, and that it chose to let you know.

events.text: The shrine of the mountain goddess on this ridge is very small and very old, and the painting inside is of an old woman with a staff. The ridge above it is scarred black where, they say, three bolts of lightning came down in one night long ago, when a fox sat in the shrine and three villages prayed to it. Beside the door, someone has stacked the firewood very neatly.

choices.text: Bow to the old woman in the painting

effects.log: You bow. You find that you are bowing lower than you meant to, as if apologising for something. The air in the shrine is very still. On the way down you meet a fox coming up with a stick of firewood in its mouth, and both of you step aside.

choices.text: Ask the shrine keeper about the woodpile

effects.log: "Nobody stacks it," the shrine keeper says. "It is always stacked. My grandmother said it was a fox that once stole the shrine and has been paying the rent ever since." The keeper grins. "Very good wood. Always dry."

events.text: The villages under the ridge have begun to pray to you. It started as a joke, because your luck is so good, and now it is not a joke: they bring you rice, and ask you for rain, and bow.

choices.text: Stop it at once, and send them to the old woman's shrine

effects.log: You send them up the ridge to the old shrine, firmly, and refuse every bow. It takes a year. When it is done you go up yourself with an armful of firewood and stack it by the door, and you do not know why, but your hands know exactly how.

choices.text: Let them, just a little

effects.log: You let them, a little. It is very pleasant. Then one clear night the sky over the ridge goes black, and wind tears at your roof, and rain, and you lie awake waiting for the third thing, and in the morning you send the villagers up to the old woman's shrine and never let anyone bow to you again.

events.text: Every summer of your life one mosquito has followed you about, the same one, you would swear, from house to field and back, whining in your ear and never once biting. This summer you are passing through a district where, the story goes, a brother once ran from his sister down this very road with four bottles from a monk, and the last one was fire.

choices.text: Stop on the road and say: I am sorry

effects.log: You stop in the road, feeling very foolish, and say out loud, to nobody: "I am sorry." The mosquito goes quiet. It sits on the back of your hand a long time, small and still in the long light. Then it goes away over the field, and for the rest of the summer you do not hear it.

choices.text: Ask in the village about the house

effects.log: The village points you to a farmhouse whose family keeps four small coloured bottles on the windowsill, empty, for luck. "Never pray for anything with the word even in it," the grandmother of the house says. "Even a fox. Heaven always hears the even." Behind you the mosquito whines and is still.

events.text: A couple in your village who have three sons have started praying at the shrine every night for a daughter: any daughter, they say, even a fox. You hear them through the shrine wall, and your skin goes cold.

choices.text: Tell them the story of the Fox Sister

effects.log: You tell them, all of it: the cattle, the brother, the bottles, the fire. They go very pale. The next night their prayer is different: a daughter, if heaven wishes, and a good one. A year later they have one, an ordinary, loud, entirely human baby girl, and you are asked to name her.

choices.text: Say only: take back the word even

effects.log: "Take back the word even," you say, and they look at you, puzzled, and then frightened, and they do. That summer, in your ear, a mosquito hums once, a different note, almost like approval.

events.text: In the capital's old market, children play a game called the dogs and the stick: one is the fox, with a red rag tucked in the belt for a tail, and all the others are dogs and salt peddlers, and the fox runs until it is caught. Watching, you feel your heart pound as if you were the one running, and you have to sit down on a step.

choices.text: Ask the children where the game comes from

effects.log: "A fox ran through here once," says the biggest, "with all the dogs in the city after it, and a salt peddler with a stick, and its tails were on fire, and it got away." "It did not get away," says a smaller one. "It did," says a third. They fight about it. You find you are hoping very hard that it did.

choices.text: Ask to be the fox

effects.log: The children are delighted to have a grown-up fox. They chase you all round the market, and you run, laughing and gasping, and they never catch you, because you know, without knowing how, every alley and every gap in every wall. At the end they all agree you were the best fox ever. You go home shaking.

events.text: A crowd in the market has caught a stranger, a quiet travelling pedlar, and is shouting that the pedlar is a fox: a dog barked, someone saw a shadow. The pedlar is very pale and very human and is being dragged toward the magistrate's gate.

choices.text: Push into the crowd and stop it

ok.log: You push in and take hold of the pedlar's arm and stand there, and something in your face makes the crowd stop. You make them look: an ordinary person, frightened, with an ordinary shadow. They go away ashamed. The pedlar shakes your hand and goes, and you sit down on the step and find you are shaking too.

fail.log: You push in and are knocked down, and trampled a little. But you slowed it, and the magistrate, coming out to see the noise, takes one look at the pedlar's ordinary shadow and sends everybody home. (-8 health)

choices.text: Shout that the dog barks at everybody

effects.log: "That dog barks at everybody!" you shout. "It barked at the magistrate last week!" People laugh, and the laughing breaks the crowd. The pedlar slips away. You did not know you could do that. Somewhere, you feel, something is very relieved.

events.text: The scholarly family you study under is descended, they say, from a student who woke. Ninety-nine sleepers before him had not, and he did, and a bead of light was in his mouth, and he kept it, and every generation since has had one scholar who can read any book once and remember it. Their family motto is: always wake.

choices.text: Ask what became of the fox

effects.log: "It lived," the eldest says, a little surprised to be asked. "Ordinary. One tail. It lay in the ditch by the school road every day for years and listened to our founder teach. When it died, the founder buried it under the school step." A pause. "The children still leave rice balls there. Nobody tells them to."

choices.text: Ask whether the bead is still in the family

effects.log: "In somebody," the eldest says. "It goes where it likes. Mostly to the one who wakes earliest." Next morning you wake before dawn, for no reason, and sit up, and the room is full of a faint pale light, and you can remember every word you read yesterday.

events.text: On the way to teach at the village school you pass an old fox lying in the ditch by the road, thin, one tail, listening to the children chant. It is there every morning. This morning, it is not getting up.

choices.text: Sit with it until it is over

effects.log: You sit with it in the ditch. The children's chanting comes down the road, sky and earth, dark and yellow. The old fox lays its head on its paws and listens to every word, and at the end of the Classic it closes its eyes. You bury it under the school step. You do not know why you weep. You suspect you have been here before.

choices.text: Carry it up to the school step, where it can hear better

effects.log: You carry it up and lay it on the warm step outside the schoolroom. The children, seeing it, chant more softly. It dies listening, very peacefully, one ear still turned to the door. The children bury it themselves, and argue about what to name it, and settle on Teacher.

events.text: A merchant is showing a rich house the White Fox Collar: white as a mourning robe, priceless, owned by a governor long ago and by eight unlucky families since. Every owner, the merchant admits, has sold it within a year, because at night it is cold, so cold, and because their dogs howl at it. When the box is opened, your throat closes, and you have to step outside.

choices.text: Buy it, at any price, and bury it (20 taels)

effects.log: Twenty taels, more than you can afford. You carry the box up into the hills to an old grave mound and bury the collar in the earth dug under it, the way foxes lie. You say the funeral words over it, for lack of others. Walking down, for the first time since you saw it, you are warm.

choices.text: Tell the rich house what it is

effects.log: You tell them: not a pelt, but somebody. A very old somebody. The rich house refuses to buy it, and the merchant curses you, and the next week, you hear, the merchant gave it free to a temple, which buried it with rites. The merchant sleeps well now, they say, for the first time in years.

choices.text: Walk away and do nothing

effects.log: You walk away. The rich house buys it. That winter their house is very cold, and their dogs howl, and in spring they sell it on, and it goes round again. You dream of it sometimes, a white shape in a dark box, waiting for somebody to take it home.

events.text: A fur trader in the market is offering twice the usual price for white fox pelts, and the hill boys are setting snares. Something in you will not let this be.

choices.text: Go round the hills and spring every snare

effects.log: You go round the hills for a week, springing snares. The boys are furious. But that winter no white fox is taken in the district, and on the first snow there is a line of white prints across your yard, very neat, going right up to your door, and stopping, and going away again.

choices.text: Tell the boys the story of the collar

effects.log: You tell them about the collar and the cold and the dogs. Boys being boys, they are delighted and terrified, and the white fox becomes the thing nobody in the district will trap, in case. The fur trader gives up and goes elsewhere. You count it a small win.

events.text: Storm-bound on an island in the West Sea, you climb to the high pool at dawn, where the islanders say the dragons of the sea once lived. In a crack of the rock above the pool, there is an arrow, very old, its feathers long gone, and you feel it in your own chest like a cold coin. The islanders say an archer left on this island once shot an old fox in a monk's robe who chanted at dawn to take the dragons' lives.

choices.text: Pull the arrow out of the rock

effects.log: It comes out of the rock with a sound like a sigh. You stand there holding it. The pool below, which was still, ripples once from the middle outward, and for one moment something long and blue-green moves in the depths, and is gone. You break the arrow and drop the pieces in the sea. Your chest stops hurting.

choices.text: Leave it, and bow to the pool

effects.log: You leave it. You bow to the pool, deeply, for something you did not do and remember doing. The water stays still. But that afternoon the storm lifts, a day early, and the islanders say the sea has decided to let you go.

events.text: Wherever you go near water, the fishermen notice: the sea is rougher for you. Wells go cloudy when you lean over them. An old fisherwoman, watching your boat pitch in a flat calm, says: "The dragons do not like you. What did you do to them?"

choices.text: Go back to the island and make an offering at the pool

effects.log: You go back with rice and wine and pour them into the pool at dawn, and kneel on the rock, and say that you are sorry, for whatever it was. The water is still a long time. Then, far down, a light moves, and the pool clears like a wiped mirror. On the way home the sea is flat and kind.

choices.text: Say you do not know, and keep away from water

effects.log: "I do not know," you say, which is true and not true. You take the mountain roads after that. In your old age, one evening at a well, the water is clear for the first time in your life, and in it you see, not your face, but a fox's, and then your own, and you think you have been forgiven, or at least forgotten.
